problems.paper_label: Round 1, Grades 10–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: Into what smallest number of non-overlapping tetrahedra can a cube be divided?

Several vectors are drawn from a point $O$ in the plane, the sum of whose lengths is $4$. Prove that one can choose several vectors (or perhaps a single vector) the length of whose sum is greater than $1$.
Prove that every even number $2n\geqslant 0$ can be represented uniquely in the form $2n=(x+y)^2+3x+y$, where $x$ and $y$ are non-negative integers.

In a triangle $ABC$ the side $BC$ is equal to half the sum of the other two sides. A circle is drawn through the point $A$ and the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, and tangents to it are drawn from the centroid of the triangle. Prove that one of the points of tangency is the centre of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$.

A pie has the shape of a regular $n$-gon inscribed in a circle of radius $1$. From the midpoints of the sides, straight cuts of length $1$ are made. Prove that some piece will then be cut off the pie.

$2n$ knights have gathered at the court of King Arthur, and each of them has among those present at most $n-1$ enemies. Prove that Merlin, Arthur's adviser, can seat the knights at a round table so that none of them sits next to his enemy.
All the coefficients of a polynomial are equal to one, zero or minus one. Prove that all its real roots (if they exist) lie in the segment from minus two to plus two.
Three points are given in the plane. Construct three circles touching one another at these points. Analyse all cases.
In the quadratic equation $x^2+px+c$ the coefficients $p$, $c$ independently run through all values from minus one to plus one inclusive. Find the set of values taken by a real root of this equation.

A circle $O$, a point $A$ lying on it, the perpendicular to the plane of the circle $O$ erected at the point $A$, and a point $B$ lying on this perpendicular are given. Find the locus of the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from the point $A$ to the lines passing through the point $B$ and an arbitrary point of the circle $O$.

Twenty cards are given. Each of the digits from zero to nine inclusive is written on two of these cards (only one digit on each card). Can these cards be arranged in a row so that the zeros are next to each other, exactly one card lies between the ones, two between the twos, and so on up to the nines, between which there must be nine cards?
Find all primes of the form $P^P+1$ ($P$ is a natural number) having at most $19$ digits.
Prove that the last digits of the numbers $n^n$ ($n$ a natural number) form a periodic sequence.
A plane $P$ and two points on different sides of it are given. Construct a sphere passing through these points that cuts the smallest circle out of $P$.

A polygon in the plane, non-convex and non-self-intersecting, is given. $D$ is the set of points belonging to those diagonals of the polygon that do not go outside it (that is, lie either entirely inside, or partly inside and partly on the boundary). The endpoints of these diagonals are also included in $D$. Prove that any two points of $D$ can be joined by a broken line lying entirely in $D$.

In each cell of a square $M\times M$ table there stands either a natural number or zero. Moreover, if a zero stands at the intersection of a row and a column, then the sum of the numbers in this row and this column is at least $M$. Prove that the sum of all the numbers in the table is at least $\frac{M^2}{2}$.

problems.paper_label: Second round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem:
Solve in positive integers the system
$$\begin{cases} x+y=zt,\\ z+t=xy.\end{cases}$$

problems.paper_label: Second round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: For what value of $K$ is the quantity $A_K=\frac{19^K+66^K}{K!}$ maximal?

problems.paper_label: Second round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: A convex pentagon is situated inside a circle (the vertices may lie either inside or on the circle). Prove that at least one of its sides is not greater than the side of the regular pentagon inscribed in this circle.

problems.paper_label: Second round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: Prove that the natural numbers $K$ for which $K^K+1$ is divisible by $30$ form an arithmetic progression. Find it.

problems.paper_label: Second round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: What is the largest number of queens that can be placed on the black squares of an $8\times 8$ chessboard so that each queen is attacked by at least one of the others? Prove that more is impossible.

problems.paper_label: Third round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: Divide a segment into $6$ equal parts with compass and ruler, drawing at most $8$ lines (straight lines and circles).

problems.paper_label: Third round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: Given: $a_1=1966$, $a_k=\left[\sqrt{a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_{k-1}}\right]$. Find $a_{1966}$. ($[A]$ denotes the integer part of $A$.)

problems.paper_label: Third round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: Of $11$ balls, two are radioactive. For any heap of balls one can find out in one check whether it contains at least one radioactive ball (but not how many). Prove that with fewer than $7$ checks it is impossible to guarantee finding both radioactive balls.

problems.paper_label: Third round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: From a set of weights of $1, 2, \ldots, 26$ select six weights such that one cannot choose from them two heaps of equal weight. Prove that one cannot choose seven weights with the same property.

problems.paper_label: Third round, Grades 9–11 (joint paper of the top classes)
problems.problem: On an $11\times 11$ checkered board $22$ cells are marked so that exactly $2$ cells are marked on each vertical and on each horizontal. Two arrangements of marked cells are equivalent if, by interchanging verticals among themselves and horizontals among themselves any number of times, one arrangement can be obtained from the other. How many non-equivalent arrangements of marked cells are there?
$K$ points ($K>2$) are situated in a square. Into what smallest number of triangles must the square be divided so that each triangle contains at most one point?
Prove that in a disc of radius $1$ one cannot find more than $5$ points all of whose pairwise distances are greater than $1$.
Prove that the equation $19x^3-17y^3=50$ has no solutions in integers.

Raisins of diameter $0.1$ are baked into an infinitely large loaf occupying the whole of space, at the points with integer coordinates. The loaf was cut into parts by several planes. Prove that there is an uncut raisin.

From the first $k$ primes $2, 3, 5, \ldots, p_k$ ($k>4$) all possible products are formed in which each of the numbers occurs at most once (for example $3\cdot 5$, $3\cdot 7\cdot\ldots\cdot p_k$, $11$, and so on). Denote the sum of all such numbers by $S$. Prove that $S+1$ factors into a product of more than $2k$ prime factors.

An $n\times n$ table and natural numbers $k$ and $m>k$ such that $m$ and $n-k$ are coprime are given. The table is filled as follows: if some row contains the numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_k, a_{k+1}, \ldots, a_m, a_{m+1}, \ldots, a_n$, then the next row contains the same numbers in the order $a_{m+1}, \ldots, a_n, a_{k+1}, \ldots, a_m, a_1, \ldots, a_k$. The numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$ are written (in order) in the first row. Prove that after the table is filled, each column contains all the numbers from $1$ to $n$.

On each side of a triangle $ABC$ a square is constructed outward ("Pythagorean trousers"). It turned out that the outer vertices of all the squares lie on one circle. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.
Can the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 12$ be arranged on a circle so that the difference between any two neighbouring numbers is $3$, $4$ or $5$?

A searchlight is installed at each of eight given points of space; each can illuminate an octant (a trihedral angle with mutually perpendicular edges) in space. Prove that the searchlights can be turned so that they illuminate the whole of space.

All possible $n$-digit numbers composed of the digits $1$, $2$ and $3$ are considered. To the end of each of these numbers a digit $1$, $2$ or $3$ is appended, in such a way that to two numbers which have different digits in every place different digits are appended. Prove that there is an $n$-digit number in whose notation only one digit $1$ occurs and to which a $1$ is appended.

$100$ aeroplanes (a flagship and $99$ auxiliary ones) take off simultaneously from a point $A$. With a full tank of fuel an aeroplane can fly $1000$ km. In flight the aeroplanes can transfer fuel to one another. An aeroplane that has given away its fuel to the others makes a gliding landing. How should the flight be carried out so that the flagship flies as far as possible?

Two players play the following game: there are two heaps of sweets. The players move in turn. A move consists in the player eating one of the heaps and dividing the other into two (equal or unequal) parts. If he cannot divide a heap because it contains only one sweet, he eats it and wins. Initially the heaps contained $33$ and $35$ sweets. Who wins, the first player or his partner, and how should he play?

Can all non-negative integers be divided into $1968$ non-empty classes so that each class contains at least one number and the following condition holds: if a number $m$ is obtained from a number $n$ by crossing out two adjacent identical digits or identical groups of digits, then $m$ and $n$ belong to the same class (for example, the numbers $7$, $9339337$, $93223393447$, $932239447$ belong to the same class)?

From a given sequence of positive numbers $q_1, \ldots, q_n, \ldots$ a sequence of polynomials is constructed as follows:
$$f_0(x)=1,\quad f_1(x)=x,\quad \ldots,\quad f_{n+1}(x)=(1+q_n)xf_n(x)-q_nf_{n-1}(x).$$
Prove that all the real roots of the $n$-th polynomial lie between $-1$ and $1$.

Four pairwise skew lines $l_1$, $l_2$, $l_3$, $l_4$ are given in space, no three of them being parallel to one plane. Draw a plane $P$ such that the points $A_1$, $A_2$, $A_3$, $A_4$ of intersection of these lines with $P$ form a parallelogram. How many lines do the centres of such parallelograms sweep out?

A circle of the largest possible radius $R$ is placed inside a convex polygon $M$ (this means that no circle of larger radius can be placed inside $M$). It is known that a segment of length $1$ can be turned inside it through any angle (i.e. we can move the unit segment as a rigid rod in the plane so that it does not go outside the polygon $M$ and is turned through any given angle). Prove that $R\geqslant 1/3$.

Some numbers are written in a $10\times 10$ table $A$. Denote the sum of all the numbers in the first row by $s_1$, in the second by $s_2$, and so on. Similarly denote the sum of the numbers in the first column by $t_1$, in the second by $t_2$, and so on. A new $10\times 10$ table $B$ is composed, with numbers written in it as follows: in the first cell of the first row the smaller of the numbers $s_1$ and $t_1$ is written, in the third cell of the fifth row the smaller of the numbers $s_5$ and $t_3$ is written, and the whole table is filled similarly. It turned out that the cells of the table $B$ can be numbered by the numbers from $1$ to $100$ so that the cell with the $k$-th number contains a number less than or equal to $k$. What is the largest value that the sum of all the numbers of the table $A$ can take under these conditions?

The system of equations
$$\begin{cases} x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_k=0,\\ x_1^3+x_2^3+\ldots+x_k^3=0,\\ \ldots\ldots\\ x_1^{19}+x_2^{19}+\ldots+x_k^{19}=0,\\ x_1^{21}+x_2^{21}+\ldots+x_k^{21}=1\end{cases}$$
is considered (all $x_i$ are real numbers). Prove that for some $k$ this system has a solution.

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is divided into $N$ convex polygons so that every line intersects at most $40$ of them (we say that a line intersects a polygon if they have a common point, for example if the line passes through a vertex of the polygon). Can $N$ be greater than a million?

$100$ distinct points are marked with chalk on the surface of a cube. Prove that the cube can be placed on a black table in two different ways (and exactly on one and the same place) so that the chalk prints on the table in these two ways are different. (If a point is marked on an edge or at a vertex, it also leaves a print.)

Two identical thin hoops are installed at the exit of a betatron; they lie in mutually perpendicular planes, and each hoop passes through the centre of the other. Particles leaving the betatron fly along a straight line through both hoops. Along what line should they move so as to be at the greatest distance from the hoops, i.e. so that the smallest distance at which the particles approach a hoop is as large as possible?

An infinite sequence of numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_n, \ldots$ is given. It is periodic with period $100$, i.e. $a_1=a_{101}$, $a_2=a_{102}$, $\ldots$. It is known that $a_1\geqslant 0$, $a_1+a_2\leqslant 0$, $a_1+a_2+a_3\geqslant 0$ and, in general, the sum $a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n$ is non-negative for odd $n$ and non-positive for even $n$. Prove that $|a_{99}|\geqslant|a_{100}|$.

A deck of punched cards of four colours is laid out in one row. If two punched cards of the same colour lie next to each other or with one card between them, one may throw away the one of them that is further to the left. In addition, one may add on the right any number of punched cards from other decks. Prove that one can add and throw away punched cards so that in the end only four of them remain.
Is there a number $h$ such that for no natural number $n$ is the number $[h\cdot 1969^n]$ divisible by $[h\cdot 1969^{n-1}]$?
A square $ABCD$ is given. Find the locus (set) of points $M$ for which the equality $\angle AMB=\angle CMD$ holds.

Two sages play the following game. The numbers $0, 1, 2, \ldots, 1024$ are written out. The first sage crosses out $512$ numbers (of his choice), the second crosses out $256$ of the remaining ones, then the first again crosses out $128$ numbers, and so on. At the tenth step the second sage crosses out one number; two numbers remain. After this the second sage pays the first the difference between these numbers. How is it more advantageous for the first sage to play? For the second? How much will the second sage pay the first if both play in the best way?

A rigid wire is bent into the shape of an equilateral triangle, and its ends are soldered. It is allowed to bend the piece of wire between any two of its points so that the bent piece becomes symmetric to its former position with respect to the line passing through these points (if these points coincide, the line through them may be drawn arbitrarily). This may be done several times. Can a regular hexagon of the same perimeter be obtained by several such operations?

A pearl of radius $3$ mm is baked into a spherical pudding of radius $20$ cm. We want to find it. For this it is allowed to cut the pudding with a sharp knife along a plane into two (equal or different) parts. If the pearl does not get under the knife, one of these parts may be cut again; if it is still not found, one of the three resulting parts may be cut, and so on. Prove that, however we cut, it may happen that after $65$ cuts the pearl is still not found. Prove that one can make $66$ cuts so that the pearl will certainly be found wherever it is.

Numbers whose sum is zero are written in the cells of an $8\times 8$ chessboard. Then each cell was divided into $4$ small compartments (by vertical and horizontal lines). Is it possible to write numbers in the compartments so that simultaneously: a) the compartments at the edge of the board contain zeros; b) for each cell the sum of the numbers standing in its four compartments is equal to the number previously written in it; c) for each node of the chessboard (where $4$ cells meet) the sum of the numbers standing in the four compartments adjacent to it is equal to zero?

It is required to arrange $1969$ cubes in a row so that some of them (a number between $0$ and $1969$) are white and the rest black, the colours being distributed approximately uniformly (see problem 5 for grade 8: if any number of consecutive cubes is marked at one place and the same number of consecutive cubes at another place, the numbers of black cubes in the two selections differ by at most $1$; moreover, if the first selection is at the left end, it contains no more black cubes than the second, and if the first selection is at the right end, it contains no fewer black cubes than the second). Prove that there are at least $1970$ different ways of arranging the cubes in a row so that these requirements are met.
The mass of each of $19$ weights is at most $70$ g and is an integer number of grams. Prove that no more than $1230$ sets of different masses can be formed from these weights.

Two non-intersecting circles $O_1$ and $O_2$ are inscribed in an angle $ABC$. $M$ is the point of tangency of $O_1$ with $BA$, $P$ the point of tangency of $O_2$ with $BC$. Prove that the circles $O_1$ and $O_2$ cut chords of equal length on the line $MP$.

The first digit of the number $2^{1970}$ was crossed out and added to the remaining number. The same operation was performed with the result, and so on, until a $10$-digit number was obtained. Prove that this number has two equal digits.

$200$ points are given in the plane, no three of which lie on one line. Can these points be numbered $1$ to $200$ so that all the hundred lines passing through the points with numbers $1$ and $101$, $2$ and $102$, $\ldots$, $100$ and $200$ pairwise intersect?

Crosses stand in some cells of a $100\times 100$ table. It is known that every row contains at least one cross, and so does every column. Prove that one can mark $10$ rows and $10$ columns so that if all the crosses in the marked columns and rows are erased, each unmarked row will still contain at least one cross, and so will each unmarked column.
A $19$-hedron is circumscribed about a sphere of radius $10$. Prove that there are two points on its surface whose distance is greater than $21$.
Prove that if a positive integer $k$ is divisible by $10\,101\,010\,101$, then at least $6$ digits of its decimal representation are nonzero.

Two spiders and a fly crawl along the edges of a transparent cube. The maximal speeds of the spider and the fly are equal. Initially the spiders were at one vertex of the cube and the fly at the opposite one. Can the spiders catch the fly? (The spiders and the fly see each other all the time.)
A natural number $n>1970$ is given. Take the remainders of the division of the number $2^n$ by $2, 3, 4, \ldots, n$. Prove that the sum of these remainders is greater than $2n$.

Merlin has two $100\times 100$ tables; one of them is empty, and on the other, magic one some numbers are written. The first table is nailed to a rock at the entrance to a cave, and the second to the wall inside the cave. You may outline on the first table some square (of size $1\times 1$, $2\times 2$, $\ldots$ or $100\times 100$) located anywhere in the table, and for a shilling learn from Merlin the sum of the numbers standing in the cells of the corresponding square of the magic table. What is the smallest amount of money needed to find out the sum of the numbers on the diagonal of the magic table?

A closed spatial broken line with vertices $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ is given; each of its links meets a fixed sphere in two points, and all the vertices of the broken line lie outside the sphere. These points divide the broken line into $3n$ segments. It is known that the segments adjacent to the vertex $A_1$ are equal to each other. The same is true for the vertices $A_2, A_3, \ldots, A_{n-1}$. Prove that the segments adjacent to the vertex $A_n$ are also equal to each other.

Petya has a "Young parquet-layer" set consisting of small boards laid in one layer in a rectangular box so that they cover its whole area. Each board has area $3$ cm$^2$ and has the shape either of a rectangle or of a corner (an L-shaped piece of three unit squares). Petya said that he had lost a board in the shape of a corner, made a rectangular board instead, and after that laid all the boards together with the new one in one layer in the box. Can one assert that he is lying?

About a sequence $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n, \ldots$ it is known that for every $n>1$ the equality $3x_n-x_{n-1}=n$ holds. Moreover, it is known that $|x_1|<1971$. Compute $x_{1971}$ with accuracy $0.000001$.

$n$ points are situated at the vertices of a convex $n$-gon. Inside this $n$-gon $k$ points are marked. It turned out that any three of the $n+k$ points do not lie on one line and are the vertices of an isosceles triangle. What can the number $k$ be equal to?

There is a heap of $10$ million matches. Two players play the following game, moving in turn. In one move a player may take from the heap a number of matches equal to $p^n$, where $p$ is a prime and $n=0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ (for example, the first takes $25$ matches, the second $8$, the first $1$, the second $5$, the first $49$, and so on). The player who takes the last match wins. Who wins with correct play?

A circle is divided into $n$ equal parts, and at the points of division numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ equal to $+1$ or $-1$ are written. If the circle is rotated through the angle $k\cdot\frac{360^\circ}{n}$, the numbers at the coinciding points are multiplied and the $n$ products obtained are added, then for every $k=1, \ldots, n-1$ this sum is equal to $0$. Prove that the number $n$ is a perfect square. What can the number $n$ be equal to?

Two sets of numbers $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ and $b_1, \ldots, b_n$ are given. Arrange the numbers $a_k$ in increasing order and the numbers $b_k$ in decreasing order. The sets $a_1^*\leqslant\ldots\leqslant a_n^*$, $b_1^*\geqslant\ldots\geqslant b_n^*$ are obtained. Prove that
$$\max(a_1+b_1, a_2+b_2, \ldots, a_n+b_n)\geqslant\max(a_1^*+b_1^*, \ldots, a_n^*+b_n^*).$$

The Banker and the Player play the following game. The Banker names a $1000$-digit number $A_1$. The Player, knowing this number, offers the Banker an arbitrary number $B_1$. After that the Banker, at his discretion, either subtracts the smaller of the numbers from the larger or adds them, and tells the Player the result, the number $A_2$. Then the Player offers the Banker the next number $B_2$. The Banker repeats the same operation with the numbers $A_2$ and $B_2$, and so on. The game ends if the Banker obtains one of the following numbers: $1, 10, 100, 1000, \ldots$. Prove that the Player can always end the game by offering the Banker at most $20$ of his numbers.

A point $O$ and $n$ pairwise non-parallel lines are given in space. The point $O$ is projected orthogonally onto all the given lines. Each of the resulting points is again projected onto all the given lines, and so on. Is there a ball containing all the points that can be obtained in this way?
Prove that the sum of the digits of a number $N$ exceeds the sum of the digits of the number $5^5\cdot N$ at most $5$ times.

$n$ inhabitants live in the town of "Diversity", any two of whom are either friends or enemies. Each day at most one inhabitant may begin a new life: quarrel with all his friends and make friends with all his enemies. Prove that all the inhabitants can become friends. (Remark. If $A$ is a friend of $B$ and $B$ is a friend of $C$, then $A$ is also a friend of $C$.)

An infinite sequence of numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n, \ldots$ is given, each next number being obtained from the preceding one by appending on the right any digit except $9$. It is known that $a_1$ is an arbitrary ten-digit number. Prove that this sequence contains at least two composite numbers.
In a tetrahedron $ABCD$ all dihedral angles are acute, and opposite edges are pairwise equal. Find the sum of the cosines of all the dihedral angles of the tetrahedron.

A non-self-intersecting non-convex $n$-gon $P$ is given. Consider the set $T$ of its interior points from which all the vertices of $P$ are visible. Prove that $T$ is a convex polygon with at most $n$ sides.

The town $X$ consists of $10$ infinite parallel avenues crossed at equal intervals by transverse streets. Two policemen, moving along the avenues and streets, try to detect a gangster who can hide behind the houses. If the gangster is on the same avenue or the same street as one of the policemen, he will be detected. The speed of the gangster exceeds the speed of the policemen at most $10$ times, and the policemen know that at the initial moment he was at a distance of at most $100$ blocks from them. Prove that the policemen can detect the gangster.

A plane $\Pi$ and a triangle $ABC$ not lying in this plane are situated in space. The triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ is the orthogonal projection of the triangle $ABC$ onto the plane $\Pi$. Prove that the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ can be covered completely by a triangle congruent to the triangle $ABC$.

Two sets of numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ and $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$ are given. It is known that: a) $x_1>x_2>\ldots>x_n>0$, $y_1>y_2>\ldots>y_n>0$; b) $x_1>y_1$, $x_1+x_2>y_1+y_2$, $\ldots$, $x_1+x_2+\ldots+x_n>y_1+y_2+\ldots+y_n$. Prove that for every natural $k$ the inequality
$$x_1^k+x_2^k+\ldots+x_n^k>y_1^k+y_2^k+\ldots+y_n^k$$
holds.

The numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 400$ are written on four hundred cards. Players $A$ and $B$ play the following game: with his first move $A$ takes any $200$ cards for himself and gives the rest to $B$. Then $B$ takes $100$ cards from each set and gives the rest to $A$; thus each player has $200$ cards. With the next move $A$ again takes $100$ cards from each set and gives the rest to $B$, and so on. After the $200$-th move of player $B$ both compute the sum of the numbers on their cards, $C_A$ and $C_B$, and $A$ pays player $B$ the difference $C_B-C_A$. What is the largest sum player $B$ can obtain if both play correctly?

Consider all the rational numbers between zero and one whose denominators do not exceed $n$. Arrange them in increasing order. Let $\frac{a}{b}$ and $\frac{c}{d}$ be some two neighbouring numbers (the fractions are irreducible). Prove that $|bc-ad|=1$.

Natural numbers are placed in all the cells of an $8\times 8$ chessboard. It is allowed to select any $3\times 3$ or $4\times 4$ square and increase all the numbers in it by $1$. We want to achieve, as a result of several such operations, that the numbers in all the cells are divisible by $10$. Can this always be done?

The following operation is performed with a natural number $K$: it is represented as a product of prime factors $K=p_1\cdot p_2\cdot\ldots\cdot p_n$; then the sum $p_1+p_2+\ldots+p_n+1$ is computed. The same is done with the resulting number, and so on. Prove that the resulting sequence is periodic from some term onwards.

A point is taken on each side of a parallelogram. The area of the quadrilateral with vertices at these points is equal to half the area of the parallelogram. Prove that at least one of the diagonals of the quadrilateral is parallel to a side of the parallelogram.
A polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients takes the values $1$, $2$ and $3$ at some integer $x$. Prove that there is at most one integer $x$ at which the value of this polynomial is equal to $5$.
Prove that every convex polyhedron has two faces with the same number of sides.

On a black box there is a display with $K$ bulbs and a control panel of $K$ two-position switches (toggles). When all possible states of the panel are run through, all possible combinations of bulbs light up successively on the display. The state of the display uniquely determines the state of the panel. It is known that whenever one toggle is switched, exactly one bulb goes out or lights up. Prove that the state of each bulb depends on the position of exactly one switch (its own for each bulb).

The number $A=\left(\frac{n+\sqrt{n^2-4}}{2}\right)^m$ is given, where $n$ and $m$ are natural numbers. Prove that there is a natural number $k$ such that
$$A=\frac{k+\sqrt{k^2-4}}{2}.$$
The bisectors of the plane angles of a trihedral angle are drawn. Prove that the pairwise angles between the bisectors are either all obtuse, or all right, or all acute.

$12$ painters live in $12$ red and white houses situated along a ring road. Each month one of the painters, taking with him a sufficient amount of white and red paint, leaves his house and walks clockwise along the ring road. On seeing a red house he paints it white and walks on, and on seeing a white house he repaints it red and goes home to wash his brushes. During the year each painter makes such a journey exactly once. Prove that at the end of the year every house will be painted in its original colour, if at the beginning of the year at least one house was red.

In a sequence consisting of zeros and ones it is allowed to interchange any two adjacent pieces of the sequence of length $5$ each. Two sequences are called similar if one of them can be obtained from the other by finitely many such transformations. How many pairwise non-similar sequences of length $100$ are there?

A lion runs on the arena of a round circus of radius $10$ metres. Moving along a broken line, it ran $30$ kilometres. Prove that the sum of all the angles through which the lion turned is at least $2998$ radians.
A triangle can be formed from segments of lengths $a$, $b$ and $c$. Prove that a triangle can also be formed from segments of lengths $\frac{1}{a+c}$, $\frac{1}{b+c}$, $\frac{1}{a+b}$.
Prove that for every $13$-gon there is a line containing exactly one of its sides, but for every $n>13$ there is an $n$-gon for which this is false.

Two identical gear wheels have $92$ teeth each. They were placed one on top of the other, and $10$ pairs of teeth were sawn off simultaneously. Prove that one wheel can be turned relative to the other so that at the places of the broken teeth of one wheel there are whole teeth of the second wheel.

The vertices and the centres of the faces of a cube are marked, and the diagonals of all the faces are drawn. Is it possible to go along the segments of these diagonals through all the marked points, visiting each of them exactly once?

A convex polygon has the following property: if all the lines on which its sides lie are moved parallel to themselves outward by the distance $1$, the resulting lines form a polygon similar to the original one, parallel sides being proportional. Prove that a circle can be inscribed in the given polygon.
Is there a sequence of natural numbers such that every natural number $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ can be represented in exactly one way as the difference of two numbers of this sequence?
Prove that the decimal representations of the numbers $2^n+1974^n$ and $1974^n$ contain the same number of digits.

A spherical planet is surrounded by $37$ point asteroids. Prove that at any moment there is a point on the surface of the planet from which an astronomer cannot observe more than $17$ asteroids. (Remark. An asteroid situated on the horizon line is not visible.)

Scientists, some of whom are friends, gathered at a congress. It turned out that any two of them who have equal numbers of friends at the congress have no common friends. Prove that there is a scientist who has exactly one friend among the participants of the congress.

A rectangular sheet of paper of size $a\times b$ cm is cut into rectangular strips each of which has a side of $1$ cm. The cutting lines are parallel to the sides of the original sheet. Prove that at least one of the numbers $a$ or $b$ is an integer.

Find all real solutions of the equation in $4$ unknowns
$$x^2+y^2+z^2+t^2=x(y+z+t).$$

A point $A$ is situated at distance $50$ cm from the centre of a disc of radius $1$ cm. It is allowed to reflect the point $A$ in an arbitrary line intersecting the disc, to reflect the resulting point in any line intersecting the disc, and so on. Prove that: a) the point $A$ can be moved inside the disc in $25$ reflections; b) this cannot be done in $24$ reflections.
Natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that the numbers $p=b^c+a$, $q=a^b+c$, $r=c^a+b$ are prime. Prove that two of the numbers $p$, $q$, $r$ are equal.
On an $8\times 8$ chessboard $64$ points are marked, the centres of all the cells. Is it possible to separate all the points from one another by drawing $13$ lines not passing through these points?
Is it possible to place four lead balls and a point light source in space so that every ray issuing from the light source meets at least one of the balls?

Kolya and Vitya play the following game. On the table there is a heap of $100$ stones. The boys move alternately, Kolya beginning. In a move the player divides each heap containing more than one stone into two smaller heaps. The player who after his move leaves heaps of one stone each wins. Can Kolya act so as to win however Vitya plays?

In the state of Mantissa towns are connected by roads. The length of every road is less than $500$ km, and from any town one can get to any other by travelling along roads less than $500$ km. When one road was closed for repairs, it turned out that from every town one could still travel along the remaining roads to any other. Prove that this can be done travelling less than $1500$ km.

The arena of a circus is lit by $n$ different searchlights. Each searchlight illuminates some convex figure. It is known that if one arbitrary searchlight is switched off, the arena will still be fully lit, but if two arbitrary searchlights are switched off, the arena will not be fully lit. For which values of $n$ is this possible?
Can some convex polygon be cut into finitely many non-convex quadrilaterals?

Find all positive solutions of the system of equations
$$\begin{cases} x_1+x_2=x_3^2,\\ x_2+x_3=x_4^2,\\ x_3+x_4=x_5^2,\\ x_4+x_5=x_1^2,\\ x_5+x_1=x_2^2.\end{cases}$$

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the median $AM$, the bisector $BK$ and the altitude $CH$ are drawn. Let $M'K'H'$ be the triangle with vertices at the points of intersection of the three drawn segments. Can the area of the resulting triangle be greater than $0.499$ of the area of the triangle $ABC$?
What are the first four digits of the number $1^1+2^2+3^3+\ldots+999^{999}+1000^{1000}$?

An astronomical searchlight illuminates an octant (a trihedral angle all of whose plane angles are right angles). The searchlight is placed at the centre of a cube. Can it be turned so that it illuminates none of the vertices of the cube?

Dominoes of size $1\times 2$ are laid on an infinite sheet of squared paper (with $1\times 1$ cells) so that they cover all the cells. Can it be achieved that every line running along the grid lines cuts only finitely many dominoes?
Is there a natural number $A$ such that if it is appended to itself on the right, the resulting number is a perfect square?
Is there a convex $1976$-hedron with the following property: for an arbitrary placement of arrows on the ends of its edges, the sum of the resulting vectors is different from $0$?

$200$ distinct numbers are placed in the cells of a $10\times 20$ table. In each row the three largest numbers are marked in red, and in each column the three largest numbers are marked in blue. Prove that at least $9$ numbers in the table are marked both red and blue.
A finite set of points is given in the plane. Prove that it contains a point which has at most three nearest points from the same set.

Each point of space is painted in one of five fixed colours, and there are $5$ points painted in different colours. Prove that there is a line whose points are painted in at least three colours, and a plane whose points are painted in at least four colours.

A sequence of natural numbers $\{x_n\}$ is constructed by the rule $x_1=2$, $x_{n+1}=[1.5x_n]$ ($[\,]$ denotes the integer part of a number).

a) Prove that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ contains infinitely many odd numbers.

b) Prove that the sequence $\{x_n\}$ contains infinitely many even numbers.

$n$ cardboard squares and $n$ plastic squares are placed on a table. No two cardboard squares have common points, including points of the boundary. The same holds for the plastic squares. It turned out that the set of vertices of the cardboard squares coincides with the set of vertices of the plastic squares. Must every cardboard square coincide with some plastic one?

a) Twelve thin rigid rods of length $1$ were fastened together so as to form the frame of a cube. Is it possible to make in a plane a hole of area less than $1/100$, not cutting the plane into pieces, such that this frame could be pulled through it?

b) The same question for the frame of a tetrahedron with edge $1$.

Each point of the number line whose coordinate is an integer is painted either red or blue. Prove that there is a colour with the following property: for every natural number $k$ there are infinitely many points of this colour whose coordinates are divisible by $k$.
Are there a) six, b) $1000$ distinct natural numbers such that for any two of them $a$ and $b$ the sum $a+b$ is divisible by the difference $a-b$?

In a volleyball tournament every two teams played one match.

a) Prove that if for any two teams there is a third one that beat both of them, then the number of teams is at least seven.

b) Construct an example of such a tournament of seven teams.

c) Prove that if for any three teams there is one that beat all three of them, then the number of teams is at least $15$.

A polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients is given such that for every natural $x$ the inequality $P(x)>x$ holds. Define the sequence $\{b_n\}$ as follows: $b_1=1$, $b_{k+1}=P(b_k)$ for $k\geqslant 1$. It is known that for every natural $d$ there is a term of the sequence $\{b_n\}$ divisible by $d$. Prove that $P(x)=x+1$.
Can an infinite set of congruent discs be placed in the plane so that every line intersects at most two discs?
A sequence of natural numbers $\{x_n\}$ is constructed by the rule $x_1=2$, $x_n=[1.5x_{n-1}]$ ($[\,]$ denotes the integer part of a number). Prove that the sequence $y_n=(-1)^{x_n}$ is non-periodic.
$12\%$ of the area of a white sphere is painted red. Prove that a parallelepiped all of whose vertices are white can be inscribed in the sphere.

A town has the shape of a square. It has $6$ streets: the $4$ sides of the square and its $2$ midlines. A policeman chases a gangster along the streets. If at some moment the policeman and the gangster are on the same street, the gangster surrenders to the policeman. Prove that the policeman can catch the gangster if his speed is: a) $3$ times greater than the speed of the gangster; b) $2.1$ times greater than the speed of the gangster.

Several lines and points are situated in the plane. Prove that there is a point $A$ in the plane, not coinciding with any of the given points, whose distance to each of the given points is greater than its distance to each of the given lines.
Prove that there exist: a) one; b) infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that the last digits of the number $2^n$ form the number $n$.
Eight real numbers $a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h$ are given. Prove that at least one of the six numbers $ac+bd$, $ae+bf$, $ag+bh$, $ce+df$, $cg+dh$, $eg+fh$ is non-negative.

There are several stones, the mass of each of which does not exceed $2$ kg, and the total mass is $100$ kg. From them several stones are chosen whose total mass differs from $10$ kg by the smallest number $d$ possible for this set. What is the largest value that the number $d$ can take over all possible sets of stones?

Several intervals are marked on a segment of length $1$. It is known that the distance between any two points belonging to one or to different marked intervals is not equal to $0.1$. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the marked intervals does not exceed $0.5$.

A function $y=f(x)$ is defined on the segment $[0;1]$ and has first and second derivatives at every point of this segment. It is known that $f(0)=f(1)=0$ and that $|f''(x)|\leqslant 1$ on the whole segment. What is the largest value that the maximum of the function $f$ can take over all functions satisfying these conditions?
The union of several discs has area $1$. Prove that one can choose from them several pairwise non-intersecting discs the sum of whose areas is greater than $\frac{1}{9}$.

$k$ scientists, chemists and alchemists, were present at a chemistry conference, and there were more chemists than alchemists. It is known that chemists always answer any question truthfully, while alchemists sometimes tell the truth and sometimes lie. A mathematician who happened to be at the conference wants to establish about each scientist whether he is a chemist or an alchemist. For this he may ask any scientist the question: "Who is such-and-such: a chemist or an alchemist?" (In particular, he may ask who this scientist himself is.) Prove that the mathematician can establish this in $2k-3$ questions.

$a_1<a_2<a_3<\ldots$ is an increasing sequence of natural numbers. It is known that for all natural $k$, $a_{k+1}$ is at most $10\cdot a_k$. Prove that the infinite decimal fraction $0.a_1a_2a_3\ldots$, obtained by writing these numbers one after another, is non-periodic.

A control panel has several buttons with which a light display is controlled. After any button is pressed, some of the bulbs of the display are switched (each button has its own set of bulbs, and the sets may intersect). Prove that the number of states in which the display can be is a power of two. (Two states of the display are different if they differ in the state of at least one bulb.)

Three straight corridors of the same length $D$ form the figure shown in the drawing (the angles between them are $120^\circ$). A gangster and a policeman run along them. The maximal speed of the policeman is twice the maximal speed of the gangster. The policeman can see the gangster if he is at distance at most $a$ from him. Prove that the policeman can always catch the gangster

a) if $a>D/5$,

b) if $a>D/7$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo_1980_0_p3_fig.png

In each cell of a $1980\times 1980$ table one of the numbers $+1$, $-1$, $0$ is written. The sum of all the numbers is $0$. Prove that there are two rows and two columns such that the sum of the four numbers standing at their intersections is equal to $0$.

Several arcs of great circles are situated on a sphere of radius one (a great circle is the intersection of the sphere with a plane passing through its centre). The sum of the lengths of all these arcs is less than $\pi$. Prove that there is a plane passing through the centre of the sphere that intersects none of these arcs.

A function $y=f(x)$ is considered, defined on the whole real axis and satisfying, for some number $k\ne 0$, the relation
$$f(x+k)\bigl(1-f(x)\bigr)=1+f(x).$$
Prove that $f$ is a periodic function.

A polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d$ with leading coefficient equal to one is given. It is known that if the argument $x$ is an integer, then $P(x)$ is an integer divisible by $m$. Prove that the number $d!$ is divisible by $m$.
Prove that the sequence $x_n=\sin(n^2)$ does not tend to zero as $n\to\infty$ through the integers.

In a square with side equal to $1$ there is a non-self-intersecting broken line of length at least $200$. Prove that there is a line parallel to one of the sides of the square that meets the broken line in at least $101$ points.
The radius of the circle inscribed in a triangle is equal to $4/3$, the lengths of the altitudes of the triangle are integers, and their sum is equal to $13$. Compute the sides of the triangle.

$n$ people sit at a round table. It is allowed to interchange any two people sitting next to each other. What is the smallest number of such interchanges that must be made so that as a result any two neighbours remain neighbours but sit in the reverse order?

a) Prove that if from some point inside a regular tetrahedron all its edges are seen at equal angles, then this point is the centre of the sphere circumscribed about the tetrahedron.

b) Are there points outside the tetrahedron from which all its edges are seen at equal angles?

Remark. If a point lies on an edge or on its extension, then this edge is considered to be seen from it at the angle $\pi$ or $0$ respectively.

a) $a$, $b$, $c$ are the lengths of the sides of a triangle. Prove that
$$a^4+b^4+c^4-2(a^2b^2+a^2c^2+b^2c^2)+a^2bc+b^2ac+c^2ab\geqslant 0.$$
b) Prove that $a^4+b^4+c^4-2(a^2b^2+a^2c^2+b^2c^2)+a^2bc+b^2ac+c^2ab\geqslant 0$ for any non-negative $a$, $b$, $c$.

Petya bought in the shop "Turing machines and other computing devices" a microcalculator that can compute $xy+x+y+1$ for any real numbers $x$ and $y$ and has no other operations. Petya wants to write a "program" for computing the polynomial $1+x+x^2+\ldots+x^{1982}$. By a "program" he means a sequence of polynomials $f_1(x), \ldots, f_n(x)$ such that $f_1(x)\equiv x$ and for every $i=2, \ldots, n$ either $f_i(x)=c_i$ (a constant) or $f_i(x)=f_j(x)\cdot f_k(x)+f_k(x)+f_j(x)+1$, where $j<i$, $k<i$, and $f_n(x)\equiv 1+x+\ldots+x^{1982}$.

a) Help Petya to write the "program".

b) Can you write a "program" if the calculator has only the single operation $xy+x+y$?
Find all natural numbers $n$ for which the numbers $\frac{1}{n}$ and $\frac{1}{n+1}$ are expressed by finite decimal fractions.
Inside a regular hexagon there is another regular hexagon with half the side. Prove that the centre of the large hexagon lies inside the small hexagon.

Let $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$ be the points at which the circle inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ touches the sides $BC$, $AC$, $AB$ respectively. It is given that $|AA_1|=|BB_1|=|CC_1|$. Prove that the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.
Prove that $4^m-4^n$ is divisible by $3^{k+1}$ if and only if $m-n$ is divisible by $3^k$. Solve the problem a) for $k=1, 2, 3$; b) for any $k$ ($m$, $n$, $k$ are natural numbers).

After a session of a mathematics circle the following record remained on the board: "Compute
$$t(0)-t\left(\frac{\pi}{5}\right)+t\left(\frac{2\pi}{5}\right)-t\left(\frac{3\pi}{5}\right)+\ldots+t\left(\frac{8\pi}{5}\right)-t\left(\frac{9\pi}{5}\right),$$
where $t(x)=\cos 5x+\ldots\cos 4x+\ldots\cos 3x+\ldots\cos 2x+\ldots\cos x+\ldots$". Seeing it, a student of the Mechanics and Mathematics Faculty told his friend that he could compute this sum even without knowing the values of the coefficients erased from the board. Is he mistaken?

In space $8$ points are chosen, no $4$ of which lie in one plane, and $17$ segments are drawn, both endpoints of each of which lie at the mentioned points. a) Prove that the segments form at least one triangle; b) prove that there are in fact at least $4$ triangles.

$13$ knights from $s$ clans ($1<s<13$) sit at a round table, and each holds a gold or a silver cup of ale, there being also $s$ gold cups. King Arthur ordered each knight to pass his cup to the neighbour on the right and to repeat this until some two knights from the same clan both receive gold cups. Prove that the king's wish will always be fulfilled (all the knights sit motionless facing the table and pass the cups so that each receives a cup from his left neighbour and passes his own cup to his right neighbour simultaneously).

Prove the inequality (without using calculators, tables and the like)
$$\sin 1<\log_3\sqrt{7}.$$

The jury of an olympiad decided to assign to each participant, according to the results, a natural number in such a way that from this number the points obtained by the participant for each problem could be recovered uniquely, and that of any two pupils the larger number is assigned to the one who obtained the larger total of points. Help the jury to solve this problem!

Solve the equation in integers
$$19x^3-84y^2=1984.$$

In a certain kingdom, in a certain state, an unlimited number of coins of denominations $n_1, n_2, n_3, \ldots$ kopecks were issued, where $n_1<n_2<n_3<\ldots$ is an infinite sequence of natural numbers. Prove that this sequence of numbers can be cut off, i.e. there is a number $N$ such that any sum that can be paid without change with the issued coins can in fact be paid with coins of denominations $n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_N$ kopecks only.
A square is cut into acute triangles. Prove that there are at least $8$ of them.
A triangular section of a cube touches the ball inscribed in the cube. Prove that the area of this section is less than half the area of a face of the cube.

Solve the equation
$$\frac{x-49}{50}+\frac{x-50}{49}=\frac{49}{x-50}+\frac{50}{x-49}.$$
The lengths $a, b, c, d$ of four segments satisfy the inequalities $0<a\leqslant b\leqslant c<d$, $d<a+b+c$. Can a trapezoid be formed from these segments?

Call the "complexity" of a given number the smallest length of a numerical sequence (if one exists) that begins with zero and ends with this number, each next term of the sequence being either equal to half of the preceding one or making $1$ together with the preceding one. Among all the numbers of the form $m/2^{50}$, where $m=1, 3, 5, \ldots, 2^{50}-1$, find the number of greatest "complexity".
$1985$ sets are given, each consisting of $45$ elements, and the union of any two sets contains exactly $89$ elements. How many elements does the union of all these $1985$ sets contain?
Prove that if the distances between the skew (opposite) edges of a tetrahedron are $h_1$, $h_2$, $h_3$ respectively, then the volume of the tetrahedron is at least $h_1h_2h_3/3$.

The points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are marked on a sheet of paper. A recognising device can perform with absolute precision two types of operations:

a) measure in centimetres the distance between two given points;

b) compare two given numbers.

What is the smallest number of operations this device must perform in order to determine for certain whether the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a square?

The bisector of the angle $A$ of a triangle $ABC$ is extended until it meets the circle circumscribed about the triangle at the point $D$. Prove the inequality
$$AD>\frac{AB+AC}{2}.$$
Solve the equation $x^{(x^4)}=4$ ($x>0$).

Prove that for no vectors $a$, $b$, $c$ can the three inequalities
$$\sqrt{3}|a|<|b-c|,\quad \sqrt{3}|b|<|c-a|,\quad \sqrt{3}|c|<|a-b|$$
hold simultaneously.

What is the smallest value, depending on the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$, that the maximum of the function
$$y(x)=|\cos x+\alpha\cos 2x+\beta\cos 3x|,\quad x\in\mathbb{R},$$
takes?

a) Prove that from any three positive numbers one can always choose two numbers $x$ and $y$ such that
$$0\leqslant\frac{x-y}{1+xy}\leqslant 1.$$
b) Is it true that such two numbers can be chosen from any four numbers?

The angles formed by the sides of an equilateral triangle with some plane are equal to $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$. Prove that one of the numbers $\sin\alpha$, $\sin\beta$, $\sin\gamma$ is equal to the sum of the other two.

$17$ unit cells are shaded on squared paper. Prove that they can be covered by rectangles the sum of whose perimeters does not exceed $100$, the distance between any points of different rectangles being at least $\sqrt{2}$.
Can the set of integers be divided into three subsets so that for every integer $n$ the numbers $n$, $n-50$, $n+1987$ belong to three different subsets?

In a certain kingdom, whose territory has the shape of a square with side $2$ km, the king decides to summon all the inhabitants to a ball in his palace at 7 p.m. For this purpose at noon he sends out a messenger, who can pass any instruction to any other inhabitant, who in turn can pass any instruction to any other inhabitant, and so on. Each inhabitant, until receiving the instruction, is at a known place (at home) and can move with speed $3$ km/h in any direction (along a straight line). Prove that the king can organise the notification so that all the inhabitants arrive in time for the beginning of the ball.

A calculator has five operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and extraction of the square root. Find a formula by which the larger of two arbitrary numbers $a$ and $b$ can be determined on this calculator.
Is there a line in the coordinate plane with respect to which the graph of the function $y=2^x$ is symmetric?
Can every parallelepiped be cut by a plane so that the section is a rectangle?

There is a ruler without divisions and a length standard that makes it possible to lay off a certain fixed distance on any already drawn line from an arbitrary point of this line. How can one draw, with these instruments and a pencil, some perpendicular to a given line?

Take a pair of natural numbers and divide the larger of them by the smaller with remainder (if the numbers are equal, also divide one of them by the other). From the quotient and the remainder obtained form a new pair of numbers and do the same with it. As soon as one of the numbers turns out to be zero, stop the computations. Prove that if one starts with numbers not exceeding $1988$, then it will not be possible to perform more than six divisions.
Solve the equation $\lg(x-2)=2x-x^2+3$.
Is there a function whose graph in the coordinate plane has a common point with every line?
Is it possible to place crosses and noughts on a sheet of squared paper so that on no horizontal, vertical or diagonal line can three identical signs in a row be found?

a) $5$; b) $1989$ distinct natural numbers are given. Prove that some infinite arithmetic progression whose first term does not exceed its common difference contains exactly $3$ or $4$ of the given numbers.
Compute, with accuracy $2$, the smallest total length of the cuts that must be made in order to recut a unit square into a rectangle with diagonal equal to $100$.

On each edge of an arbitrary tetrahedron a point is chosen. Through each triple of points lying on edges with a common vertex a plane is drawn. Prove that if three of the four planes drawn touch the ball inscribed in the tetrahedron, then the fourth plane also touches it.

Find the largest value of the expression
$$x\sqrt{1-y^2}+y\sqrt{1-x^2}.$$

Prove that if a function $f(x)$ defined on the segment $[0,1]$ is continuous and satisfies the identity $f(f(x))\equiv x^2$, then the estimates
$$x^2<f(x)<x,\quad x\in(0,1),$$
hold. Give an example of such a function.
In a triangle $ABC$ the median $BD$ and the bisector $BE$ are drawn. Can it happen that $BD$ is a bisector in the triangle $BCE$, and $BE$ is a median in the triangle $ABD$?
Prove that for every odd number there is a multiple of it whose decimal representation consists only of odd digits.
For what arrangement of $4$ points in space can they be the projections of some point onto the $4$ planes of the faces of some tetrahedron, respectively?

Between which two nines in the number
$$1\underbrace{99\ldots 9}_{1991\text{ nines}}1$$
should a sign be placed:

a) "$+$", so that the resulting sum is the smallest;

b) "$\times$", so that the resulting product is the largest?
