The figure shows an orthogonal projection of the globe with the equator ($A$ and $B$ are the common points of the projection of the equator with the circle). How can one find the projection of the North Pole using compass and ruler?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo_1991_0_p2_fig.png
Prove that in a regular $54$-gon there are four diagonals not passing through its centre that meet at one point (different from a vertex).

A council of $2000$ deputies decided to approve the state budget, containing $200$ items of expenditure. Each deputy prepared his own draft budget, in which he indicated for each item the maximal admissible (in his opinion) amount of expenditure, making sure that the total amount of expenditure did not exceed a given value $S$. For each item the council approves the largest amount of expenditure that at least $k$ deputies agree to allocate. For what smallest $k$ can it be guaranteed that the total amount of approved expenditure does not exceed $S$?

On a rectangular $m\times n$ screen divided into unit cells, more than $(m-1)(n-1)$ cells are lit. If in some $2\times 2$ square three cells are not lit, then after some time the fourth one also goes out. Prove that nevertheless at least one cell on the screen will always remain lit.
It is required to fill a square $n\times n$ table with numbers so that the sum of the numbers on each of the $4n-2$ diagonals is equal to $1$. Can this be done for: a) $n=55$; b) $n=1992$?
Find the angles of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ in which $\angle BAC=30^\circ$, $\angle ACD=40^\circ$, $\angle ADB=50^\circ$, $\angle CBD=60^\circ$ and $\angle ABC+\angle ADC>180^\circ$.

Aladdin visited every point of the equator, moving now east, now west, and sometimes instantly moving to the diametrically opposite point of the Earth. Prove that there was a period of time during which the difference between the distances travelled by Aladdin eastward and westward was at least half the length of the equator.
Can the edges of a convex polyhedron always be coloured in two colours so that for every face the numbers of edges of the two colours differ by at most $1$?
It is known that $\operatorname{tg}A+\operatorname{tg}B=p$ and $\operatorname{ctg}A+\operatorname{ctg}B=q$. Find $\operatorname{tg}(A+B)$.
A unit square is divided into a finite number of smaller squares (whose sizes may differ). Can the sum of the perimeters of the small squares that intersect the main diagonal be greater than $1993$?
$n$ points are given in the plane, no three of which lie on one line. Through every pair of points a line is drawn. What is the smallest possible number of pairwise non-parallel lines among them?

a) It is known that the domain of a function $f(x)$ is the segment $[-1,1]$, that $f(f(x))=-x$ for all $x$, and that its graph is the union of finitely many points and intervals. Draw the graph of the function $f(x)$.

b) Can this be done if the domain of the function is the interval $(-1,1)$? The whole number line?
A fly flies inside a regular tetrahedron with edge $a$. What is the smallest distance it must fly in order to visit every face and return to the starting point?
Devise a polyhedron that has no three faces with the same number of sides.

An infinite sequence of numbers $x_n$ is defined by the conditions $x_{n+1}=1-|1-2x_n|$, with $0\leqslant x_1\leqslant 1$. Prove that the sequence is periodic from some term onwards a) if and b) only if $x_1$ is rational.

A cherry, a ball of radius $r$, is dropped into a round wine glass whose axial section is the graph of the function $y=x^4$. For what largest $r$ will the ball touch the lowest point of the bottom? (In other words, what is the largest radius $r$ of a disc lying in the region $y\geqslant x^4$ and containing the origin?)

From a convex polyhedron with $9$ vertices, one of which is $A$, $8$ polyhedra congruent to it are obtained by the parallel translations taking $A$ to each of the other vertices. Prove that at least two of these $8$ polyhedra intersect (in interior points).

The extensions of the sides $AB$ and $CD$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at the point $P$, and the extensions of the sides $BC$ and $AD$ meet at the point $Q$. Prove that if each of the three pairs of bisectors — of the exterior angles of the quadrilateral at the vertices $A$ and $C$, of the exterior angles at the vertices $B$ and $D$, and of the exterior angles at the vertices $Q$ and $P$ (of the triangles $QAB$ and $PBC$ respectively) — has a point of intersection, then these three points lie on one line.
Prove that for every $k>1$ there is a power of $2$ such that among its last $k$ digits at least half are nines. (For example, $2^{12}=\ldots 4096$, $2^{53}=\ldots 992$.)
Prove that $|x|+|y|+|z|\leqslant|x+y-z|+|x-y+z|+|-x+y+z|$, where $x$, $y$, $z$ are real numbers.
In a triangle $ABC$, $AA_1$ is a median, $AA_2$ is an angle bisector, and $K$ is a point on $AA_1$ such that $KA_2\parallel AC$. Prove that $AA_2\perp KC$.

Cut the segment $[-1;1]$ into black and white segments so that the integrals of any

a) linear function;

b) quadratic trinomial

over the white and over the black segments are equal.

For what largest $n$ can one devise two sequences $A$ and $B$, infinite in both directions, such that every piece of the sequence $B$ of length at most $n$ is contained in $A$, $A$ has period $1995$, and $B$ does not have this property (it is non-periodic or has a period of a different length)?
Prove that there are infinitely many composite $n$ such that $3^{n-1}-2^{n-1}$ is divisible by $n$.
Is there a polyhedron and a point outside it such that none of its vertices is visible from this point?
Positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that $a^2+b^2-ab=c^2$. Prove that $(a-c)(b-c)\leqslant 0$.
problems.proposer: V. O. Bugaenko, A. A. Egorov

problems.problem: Find some polynomial with integer coefficients one of whose roots is the number $\sqrt[5]{2+\sqrt{3}}+\sqrt[5]{2-\sqrt{3}}$.
Eight parallel planes are given in space such that the distances between any two neighbouring ones are equal. A point is chosen on each of the planes. Can the chosen points be the vertices of a cube?
Prove that there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ such that the number $n$ can be represented as a sum of squares of two natural numbers, while the numbers $n-1$ and $n+1$ cannot.

A point $X$ lying outside the non-intersecting circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ is such that the segments of the tangents drawn from $X$ to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are equal. Prove that the point of intersection of the diagonals of the quadrilateral formed by the points of tangency coincides with the point of intersection of the common internal tangents to $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$.

In a $2^n\times n$ table all possible rows of length $n$ consisting of the numbers $1$ and $-1$ were written. Then some of the numbers were replaced by zeros. Prove that one can choose several rows whose sum is the row of zeros. (The sum of rows is the row whose entries are the sums of the corresponding entries of the summands.)

On the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ of a triangle $ABC$ the points $C'$, $A'$ and $B'$ respectively are taken. Prove that the area of the triangle $A'B'C'$ is equal to
$$\frac{AB'\cdot BC'\cdot CA'+AC'\cdot CB'\cdot BA'}{4R},$$
where $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.

Compute
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(\cos^2(\cos x)+\sin^2(\sin x)\right)dx.$$

A teacher wrote three functions on the board: $f_1(x)=x+\frac{1}{x}$, $f_2(x)=x^2$, $f_3(x)=(x-1)^2$, and suggested that the pupils obtain the function $\frac{1}{x}$ using the operations of addition, multiplication, subtraction, multiplication by an arbitrary number and addition of an arbitrary number. Carry out this task and prove that all three functions must be used in doing so.
Is it possible to divide a regular tetrahedron with edge $1$ into regular tetrahedra and octahedra the lengths of whose edges are less than $1/100$?

Positive numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that $abc=1$. Prove that
$$\frac{1}{1+a+b}+\frac{1}{1+b+c}+\frac{1}{1+c+a}\leqslant 1.$$
A finite number of strips, the sum of whose widths is $100$, and a disc of radius $1$ are given in the plane. Prove that each of the strips can be translated so that together they cover the disc.

The numbers $x, y, z$ satisfy the equality
$$x+y+z-2(xy+yz+xz)+4xyz=1/2.$$
Prove that at least one of them is equal to $1/2$.
In a non-isosceles triangle $ABC$ the medians $AK$ and $BL$ are drawn. The angles $\angle BAK$ and $\angle CBL$ are equal to $30^\circ$. Find the angles of the triangle $ABC$.
Solve in natural numbers the equation $3^x+4^y=5^z$.

The natural numbers from $1$ to $n$ are arranged in a row in an arbitrary order (the number $n$ is fixed). An arrangement is called bad if one can mark in it $10$ numbers (not necessarily standing consecutively) going in decreasing order. The other arrangements are called good. Prove that the number of good arrangements does not exceed $81^n$.

$a, b, c$ are the sides of a triangle. Prove the inequality
$$\frac{a^2+2bc}{b^2+c^2}+\frac{b^2+2ac}{c^2+a^2}+\frac{c^2+2ab}{a^2+b^2}>3.$$

A plane convex figure is bounded by the segments $AB$ and $AC$ and the arc $BC$ of some circle (see the figure). Construct some line that bisects: a) the perimeter of this figure; b) its area.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo_1999_0_p2_fig.png

The faces of a regular octahedron are painted white and black, any two faces having a common edge being painted in different colours. Prove that for every point inside the octahedron the sum of the distances to the planes of the white faces is equal to the sum of the distances to the planes of the black faces.

A meadow in the shape of a square has a round hole in it. A grasshopper jumps about the meadow. Before each jump it chooses a vertex and jumps in its direction; the length of the jump is equal to half the distance to this vertex. Can the grasshopper get into the hole?

A graph is a set of vertices some of which are joined by edges (each edge joins exactly two vertices of the graph). A colouring of the vertices of a graph is called proper if vertices of the same colour are not joined by an edge. Some graph is properly coloured in $k$ colours, and it cannot be properly coloured in a smaller number of colours. Prove that in this graph there is a path along which vertices of all $k$ colours occur exactly once each.
Solve in natural numbers the equation $(1+n^k)^l=1+n^m$, where $l>1$.
Prove that the first digits of the numbers of the form $2^{2^n}$ form a non-periodic sequence.
The greatest common divisor (gcd) of natural numbers $m$ and $n$ is $1$. What is the largest possible value of the gcd of the numbers $m+2000n$ and $n+2000m$?

Compute
$$\int_0^{\pi}\left(|\sin 1999x|-|\sin 2000x|\right)dx.$$

Chords $AC$ and $BD$ of a circle with centre $O$ meet at the point $K$. Let $M$ and $N$ be the centres of the circles circumscribed about the triangles $AKB$ and $CKD$ respectively. Prove that $OM=KN$.

Fedya has three sticks. If a triangle cannot be formed from them, Fedya shortens the longest stick by the sum of the lengths of the other two. If the length of the stick has not become zero and again no triangle can be formed, Fedya repeats the operation, and so on. Can this process go on forever?
Is it possible to place infinitely many congruent convex polyhedra in a layer bounded by two parallel planes so that no polyhedron can be taken out of the layer without moving the others?
Do there exist three quadratic trinomials such that each of them has two distinct real roots, while the sum of any two of the trinomials has no real roots?
A geometric progression is given. It is known that its first, tenth and thirtieth terms are natural numbers. Is it true that its twentieth term is also a natural number?

In a triangle $ABC$ the point $I$ is the centre of the inscribed circle, $I'$ is the centre of the circle touching the side $AB$ and the extensions of the sides $CB$ and $CA$; $L$ and $L'$ are the points at which the side $AB$ touches these circles. Prove that the lines $IL'$, $I'L$ and the altitude $CH$ of the triangle $ABC$ meet at one point.
Prove that there is no polynomial of degree at least two with non-negative integer coefficients whose value at every prime $p$ is a prime number.

Prove that there is an arrangement in space of $2001$ convex polyhedra such that no three of the polyhedra have common points, while any two touch each other (i.e. have at least one common boundary point but no common interior points).

Several boxes are arranged in a circle. Each of them may contain one or several balls (or it may be empty). In one move one may take all the balls from any box and distribute them, moving clockwise and starting with the next box, putting one ball into each box.

a) Prove that if at each following move the balls are taken from the box into which the last ball fell at the preceding move, then at some moment the initial arrangement of the balls is repeated.

b) Prove that in several moves one can obtain from any initial arrangement of the balls in the boxes any other one.
The tangents of the angles of a triangle are natural numbers. What can these numbers be equal to?
Prove that one can mark on the graph of the function $y=x^3$ a point $A$, and on the graph of the function $y=x^3+|x|+1$ a point $B$, such that the distance $AB$ does not exceed $1/100$.

Every spectator who bought a ticket for the first row of a cinema took one of the seats in the first row. It turned out that all the seats of the first row are occupied, but every spectator is sitting in a seat that is not his own. The usher can interchange neighbours if both are sitting in seats that are not their own. Can he always seat everybody in their own seats?

In an increasing sequence of natural numbers every number, starting from the $2002$-nd, is a divisor of the sum of all the preceding numbers. Prove that the sequence contains some number starting from which every number is equal to the sum of all the preceding ones.

Let $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ be the altitudes of an acute triangle $ABC$; $O_A$, $O_B$, $O_C$ the centres of the circles inscribed in the triangles $AB_1C_1$, $BC_1A_1$, $CA_1B_1$ respectively; $T_A$, $T_B$, $T_C$ the points of tangency of the circle inscribed in the triangle $ABC$ with the sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ respectively. Prove that all the sides of the hexagon $T_AO_CT_BO_AT_CO_B$ are equal.

In the town of Udoev the mayor is elected as follows. If in a round of voting none of the candidates has received more than half of the votes, the next round is held with all the candidates except the one who came last by the number of votes. (No two candidates ever receive equal numbers of votes; if a candidate receives more than half of the votes, he becomes mayor and the election ends.) In each round every voter votes for one of the candidates. If this candidate has passed into the next round, the voter votes for him again. If the candidate has dropped out, all his voters vote for one and the same candidate from among the remaining ones.

At the latest election $2002$ candidates stood. Ostap Bender, who took the $k$-th place by the number of votes in the first round, became mayor. Determine the largest possible value of $k$ if Ostap was elected

a) in the $1002$-nd round;

b) in the $1001$-st round.

For positive numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ the equality
$$\frac{x^2}{y}+\frac{y^2}{z}+\frac{z^2}{x}=\frac{x^2}{z}+\frac{z^2}{y}+\frac{y^2}{x}$$
holds. Prove that at least two of the numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ are equal.

A polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $2003$ with real coefficients and leading coefficient $1$ is given. There is an infinite sequence of integers $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ such that $P(a_1)=0$, $P(a_2)=a_1$, $P(a_3)=a_2$ and so on. Prove that not all the numbers of the sequence $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ are distinct.

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. The points $P$ and $Q$ are symmetric to the point $C$ with respect to the lines $AB$ and $AD$ respectively. Prove that the line $PQ$ passes through the orthocentre (the point of intersection of the altitudes) $H$ of the triangle $ABD$.

On the perimeter of a round cake of diameter $n/\pi$ metres there are $n$ cherries. If there are cherries at the endpoints of some arc, then the number of the other cherries on this arc is less than the length of the arc in metres. Prove that the cake can be cut into $n$ equal sectors so that each piece contains one cherry.
In a convex polyhedron the interior dihedral angle at each edge is acute. How many faces can the polyhedron have?
problems.proposer: O. K. Podlipsky, A. A. Zaslavsky

problems.problem: On the shore of the round island of Gdetotam there are $20$ villages, each inhabited by $20$ wrestlers. A tournament was held in which every wrestler met all the wrestlers from all the other villages. Village $A$ is considered stronger than village $B$ if at least $k$ bouts between wrestlers from these villages end in a victory of the wrestler from village $A$. It turned out that each village is stronger than the next one clockwise. What is the largest possible value of $k$? (All wrestlers have different strengths, and in a bout the stronger one always wins.)

The equality
$$(a^{m_1}-1)\ldots(a^{m_n}-1)=(a^{k_1}+1)\ldots(a^{k_l}+1)$$
is given, where $a$, $n$, $l$ and all the exponents are natural numbers, and $a>1$. Find all possible values of the number $a$.
Prove that every quadratic trinomial can be represented as the sum of two quadratic trinomials with zero discriminants.
Is it true that for any four pairwise skew lines one can choose one point on each of them so that these points are the vertices of a) a trapezoid, b) a parallelogram?

Prove that for every natural number $d$ there is a natural number $n$ divisible by it in whose decimal representation one can cross out some nonzero digit so that the resulting number is also divisible by $d$.

A triangle $ABC$ with acute angle $\angle A=\alpha$ is inscribed in a circle. A diameter of this circle passes through the foot of the altitude of the triangle drawn from the vertex $B$ and divides the triangle $ABC$ into two parts of equal area. Find the angle $B$.

For given natural numbers $k_0<k_1<k_2$ determine the smallest number of roots on the interval $[0;2\pi)$ that an equation of the form
$$\sin k_0x+A_1\sin k_1x+A_2\sin k_2x=0,$$
where $A_1, A_2\in\mathbb{R}$, can have.

Two guards walk clockwise along the wall of a round tower, the first of them twice as fast as the second. Loopholes are made in this wall, which has length $1$. A system of loopholes is called reliable if, for some initial position of the guards, at every subsequent moment of time at least one of them is near a loophole.

a) What is the smallest length a loophole can have if the system consisting of this loophole alone is reliable?

b) Prove that the total length of the loopholes of any reliable system is greater than $1/2$.

c) Prove that for every number $s>1/2$ there is a reliable system of loopholes of total length less than $s$.

The numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that the first equation of the system
$$\begin{cases}\sin x+a=bx,\\ \cos x=b\end{cases}$$
has exactly two solutions. Prove that the system has at least one solution.
problems.proposer: after T. Golenishcheva-Kutuzova and I. Yashchenko

problems.problem: The sum of the absolute values of the terms of a finite arithmetic progression is $100$. If all its terms are increased by $1$, or all its terms are increased by $2$, then in both cases the sum of the absolute values of the terms of the resulting progression is also $100$. What values can the quantity $n^2d$ take under these conditions, where $d$ is the common difference of the progression and $n$ is the number of its terms?

A $2005\times 2005$ board is divided into unit square cells. Some cells of the board are numbered in some order by the numbers $1, 2, \ldots$ so that at distance less than $10$ from every unnumbered cell there is a numbered cell. Prove that there are two cells at distance less than $150$ that are numbered by numbers differing by more than $23$. The distance between cells is the distance between their centres.

Two two-digit numbers were successively appended on the right to some natural number. The resulting number turned out to be equal to the cube of the sum of the three original numbers. Find all possible triples of original numbers.

A circle is drawn on a rectangular sheet of paper; inside it Misha mentally chooses $n$ points, and Kolya tries to guess them. In one attempt Kolya points to one point of the sheet (inside or outside the circle), and Misha tells Kolya the distance from it to the nearest unguessed point. If it turns out to be zero, then after that the indicated point is considered guessed. Kolya can mark points on the sheet, lay off distances and perform constructions with compass and ruler. Can Kolya be sure to guess all the chosen points in fewer than $(n+1)^2$ attempts?

The numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that the first equation of the system
$$\begin{cases}\cos x=ax+b,\\ \sin x+a=0\end{cases}$$
has exactly two solutions. Prove that the system has at least one solution.
problems.proposer: after T. Golenishcheva-Kutuzova and I. Yashchenko

problems.problem: The sum of the absolute values of the terms of a finite arithmetic progression is $250$. If all its terms are decreased by $1$, or all its terms are decreased by $2$, then in both cases the sum of the absolute values of the terms of the resulting progression is also $250$. What values can the quantity $n^2d$ take under these conditions, where $d$ is the common difference of the progression and $n$ is the number of its terms?

A $2005\times 2005$ board is divided into unit square cells. Some cells of the board are numbered in some order by the numbers $1, 2, \ldots$ so that at distance less than $5$ from every unnumbered cell there is a numbered cell. Prove that there are two cells at distance less than $100$ that are numbered by numbers differing by more than $34$. The distance between cells is the distance between their centres.

Two two-digit numbers were successively appended on the right to some natural number. The resulting number turned out to be equal to the cube of the sum of the three original numbers. Find all possible triples of original numbers.

A circle is drawn on a rectangular sheet of paper; inside it Kolya mentally chooses $n$ points, and Misha tries to guess them. In one attempt Misha points to one point of the sheet (inside or outside the circle), and Kolya tells Misha the distance from it to the nearest unguessed point. If it turns out to be zero, then after that the indicated point is considered guessed. Misha can mark points on the sheet, lay off distances and perform constructions with compass and ruler. Can Misha be sure to guess all the chosen points in fewer than $(n+1)^2$ attempts?

What values can the common difference of an increasing arithmetic progression $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots, \alpha_5$ take, all of whose terms belong to the segment $[0;3\pi/2]$, if the numbers $\cos\alpha_1$, $\cos\alpha_2$ and $\cos\alpha_3$, as well as the numbers $\sin\alpha_3$, $\sin\alpha_4$ and $\sin\alpha_5$, taken in some order, also form arithmetic progressions?
Find all irreducible fractions $a/b$ representable in the form $\overline{b,a}$ (the decimal comma separates the decimal representations of the natural numbers $b$ and $a$).

Can an inextensible ribbon be wound onto an infinite cone so as to make infinitely many turns around its axis? The ribbon may not be wound over the vertex of the cone, nor may it be cut or twisted. If necessary one may assume that it is infinite and that the angle between the axis and a generatrix of the cone is sufficiently small.

Alice and Basilio play the following game: from a bag initially containing $1331$ coins they take coins in turn, Alice making the first move and taking $1$ coin, and then at each following move the player takes (at his or her discretion) either the same number of coins as the other player took at the last move, or one more. The player who cannot make a move according to the rules loses. Which of the players can ensure a win regardless of the moves of the other?

A point is fixed on the bisector of a given angle. All possible isosceles triangles are considered whose apex is at this point and whose base endpoints lie on different sides of this angle. Find the locus of the midpoints of the bases of such triangles.

All the sweets of different kinds available in a warehouse are distributed among $n$ boxes, for which prices of $1, 2, \ldots, n$ conventional units respectively are set. It is required to buy $k$ of these boxes of least total cost that are certain to contain at least $k/n$ of the mass of all the sweets, under the sole condition that the mass of sweets in any box does not exceed the mass of sweets in any more expensive box.

a) Which boxes should be bought for $n=10$ and $k=3$?

b) The same question for arbitrary natural $n\geqslant k$.

A round target is divided into $20$ sectors, which are numbered around the circle in some order by the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 20$. If the sectors are numbered, for example (as in darts), in the order
$$1, 20, 5, 12, 9, 14, 11, 8, 16, 7, 19, 3, 17, 2, 15, 10, 6, 13, 4, 18,$$
then the smallest of the differences between the numbers of neighbouring (around the circle) sectors is $12-9=3$ (the smaller number is subtracted from the larger). Can this quantity be greater than $3$ for a numbering in another order? What is the largest possible value of this quantity?

The value of $a$ is chosen so that the number of roots of the first of the equations
$$4^x-4^{-x}=2\cos ax,\qquad 4^x+4^{-x}=2\cos ax+4$$
is equal to $2007$. How many roots does the second equation have for the same $a$?
What can the product of several distinct primes be if it is divisible by each of them decreased by $1$? Find all possible values of this product.

A point $O$ lies in the base $A_1A_2\ldots A_n$ of a pyramid $SA_1A_2\ldots A_n$, with $SA_1=SA_2=\ldots=SA_n$ and $\angle SA_1O=\angle SA_2O=\ldots=\angle SA_nO$. For what smallest value of $n$ does it follow from this that $SO$ is the altitude of the pyramid?

A square consists of $n\times n$ cells: two opposite corner cells are black and the others are white. What is the smallest number of white cells that it suffices to repaint black so that after this, by means of transformations consisting of repainting all the cells of some column or some row in the opposite colour, all the cells of the square can be made black?

The points $A'$, $B'$ and $C'$ are the midpoints of the sides $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ of a triangle $ABC$, and $BH$ is its altitude. Prove that if the circles circumscribed about the triangles $AHC'$ and $CHA'$ pass through a point $M$ different from $H$, then $\angle ABM=\angle CBB'$.

The numbers $p$ and $q$ are such that the parabolas $y=-2x^2$ and $y=x^2+px+q$ intersect in two points, bounding some figure. Find the equation of the vertical line dividing the area of this figure in half.
Find the smallest natural $n$ for which the number $n^n$ is not a divisor of the number $2008!=1\cdot 2\cdot\ldots\cdot 2008$.

In the unified examination $333$ pupils made $1000$ mistakes in total. Is it possible that the number of pupils who made more than $5$ mistakes each was greater than the number of pupils who made fewer than $4$ mistakes each?

Through the centre $O$ of the circle inscribed in a triangle $ABC$ a line is drawn perpendicular to the line $AO$ and meeting the line $BC$ at the point $M$. From the point $O$ the perpendicular $OD$ is dropped to the line $AM$. Prove that the points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ lie on one circle.

A machine tool produces parts of two types. On the belt of its conveyor $75$ parts are laid out in one line. While the conveyor is moving, the machine prepares a part of the type of which there are fewer on the belt. Every minute the next part falls off the belt, and the prepared one is placed at its end. Some number of minutes after the conveyor is switched on it may happen that the arrangement of the parts on the belt repeats the initial one for the first time. Find: a) the smallest such number, b) all such numbers.

A player at a computer controls a fox hunting two hares. At the vertex $A$ of a square $ABCD$ there is a burrow: if at least one hare gets into it in the absence of the fox, the game is lost. The fox catches a hare as soon as it is at the same point as the hare (possibly at the point $A$). Initially the fox sits at the point $C$, and the hares at the points $B$ and $D$. The fox runs everywhere with speed at most $v$, and the hares run along the rays $AB$ and $AD$ with speed at most $1$. For what values of $v$ will the fox be able to catch both hares?

Is it possible, among the vertices of any polyhedron, to choose four vertices of a tetrahedron the area of whose projection onto any plane is a) more than $\frac{1}{4}$, b) at least $\frac{1}{9}$, c) at least $\frac{1}{7}$ of the area of the projection (onto the same plane) of the original polyhedron?

When water is drained from a pool, the water level $h$ in it changes with time $t$ according to the law
$$h(t)=at^2+bt+c,$$
and at the moment $t_0$ when the draining ends the equalities $h(t_0)=h'(t_0)=0$ hold. In how many hours does the water drain from the pool completely, if during the first hour the water level in it is halved?

A skein of thread was pierced right through by $72$ cylindrical knitting needles, each of radius $1$, as a result of which it took the form of a cylinder of radius $6$. Could the height of this cylinder also be equal to $6$?

In the plane coordinate axes with the same, but not marked, scale are given, together with the graph of the function
$$y=\sin x,\quad x\in(0;\alpha).$$
How can one construct with compass and ruler the tangent to this graph at a given point of it, if: a) $\alpha\in\left(\frac{\pi}{2};\pi\right)$; b) $\alpha\in\left(0;\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$?

Through each vertex of a quadrilateral a line is drawn passing through the centre of the circle inscribed in it. Three of these lines have the property that each of them divides the area of the quadrilateral into two equal parts.

a) Prove that the fourth line also has this property.

b) What values can the angles of this quadrilateral take if one of them is equal to $72^\circ$?
For each prime $p$ find the largest natural power of the number $p!$ by which the number $(p^2)!$ is divisible.

Prove that for every partition of the hundred "two-digit" numbers $00, 01, \ldots, 99$ into two groups, some numbers of at least one group can be written in a row so that any two neighbouring numbers of this row differ from each other by $1$, $10$ or $11$, and in at least one of the two places (units or tens) all $10$ different digits occur.

What is the largest value that the expression
$$1:(a+2010:(b+1:c))$$
can take, where $a$, $b$, $c$ are pairwise distinct nonzero digits?

In a square sandpit filled with an even layer of sand of height $1$, Masha and Pasha made sand pies using a cylindrical bucket of height $2$. All of Masha's pies came out well, while Pasha's crumbled and turned into cones of the same height. In the end all the sand went into the pies, placed on the bottom of the sandpit separately from one another. Whose pies were there more of in the sandpit: Masha's or Pasha's?

Prove that if the numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ are, for some values of $p$ and $q$, solutions of the system
$$\begin{cases} y=x^n+px+q,\\ z=y^n+py+q,\\ x=z^n+pz+q,\end{cases}$$
then the inequality $x^2y+y^2z+z^2x\geqslant x^2z+y^2x+z^2y$ holds, where a) $n=2$; b) $n=2010$.

A function $f$ assigns to each vector $v$ (with common origin at the point $O$) of space a number $f(v)$, such that for any vectors $u$, $v$ and any numbers $\alpha$, $\beta$ the value $f(\alpha u+\beta v)$ does not exceed at least one of the numbers $f(u)$ or $f(v)$. What is the largest number of values that such a function can take?
Inside a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ a point $P$ is taken such that $\angle PBA=\angle PCD=90^\circ$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $AD$, and $BM=CM$. Prove that $\angle PAB=\angle PDC$.

A sequence of two distinct numbers was continued in two ways: so as to obtain a geometric progression, and so as to obtain an arithmetic progression. The third term of the geometric progression coincided with the tenth term of the arithmetic progression. With which term of the arithmetic progression did the fourth term of the geometric progression coincide?
Compare the smallest positive roots of the polynomials $x^{2011}+2011x-1$ and $x^{2011}-2011x+1$.

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ a point $D$ is taken on the base $BC$, and points $E$ and $M$ on the lateral side $AB$, such that $AM=ME$ and the segment $DM$ is parallel to the side $AC$. Prove that $AD+DE>AB+BE$.

A real number is written in each cell of a square table. It is known that in each row of the table the sum of the $k$ largest numbers is $a$, and in each column of the table the sum of the $k$ largest numbers is $b$.

1) Prove that if $k=2$, then $a=b$.

2) In the case $k=3$ give an example of such a table for which $a\ne b$.

The orthogonal projections of a given regular tetrahedron with unit edge onto all possible planes are considered. What is the largest value that the radius of a disc contained in such a projection can take?

A seller wants to cut a piece of cheese into parts that can be put into two heaps of equal weight. He can cut any piece of cheese in one and the same ratio $a:(1-a)$ by weight, where $0<a<1$. Is it true that on every interval of length $0.001$ in the interval $(0;1)$ there is a value of $a$ for which he will be able to achieve the desired result by a finite number of cuts?

A curve in the plane is, in some (Cartesian) coordinate system, the graph of the function $y=\sin x$. Can the same curve be the graph of the function $y=\sin^2x$ in another coordinate system? If so, what are its origin and the units of length on the axes (relative to the original coordinates and units of length)?

Is it true that any $100$ cards, on each of which one digit $1$, $2$ or $3$ is written, each digit occurring at most $50$ times, can be laid out in a row so that it contains no fragments $11$, $22$, $33$, $123$ and $321$?

Inside a triangle $ABC$ a point $O$ is taken such that
$$\angle ABO=\angle CAO,\quad \angle BAO=\angle BCO,\quad \angle BOC=90^\circ.$$
Find the ratio $AC:OC$.

For which permutation $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2011}$ of the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 2011$ will the value of the expression
$$a_1^{a_2^{a_3^{\cdot^{\cdot^{\cdot^{a_{2010}^{a_{2011}}}}}}}}$$
be the largest?

Four beetles crawl along the edges of a triangular pyramid, each beetle always remaining on just one face (each face has its own beetle). Each beetle goes around the boundary of its face in a certain direction, and any two beetles crawl along their common edge in opposite directions. Prove that if the speeds (possibly non-constant) of each of the beetles are always greater than $1$ cm/s, then sooner or later some two beetles will necessarily meet, regardless of the pyramid, the initial position and the speeds of the beetles.

Alyosha wrote on the board $5$ integers: the coefficients and the roots of a quadratic trinomial. Borya erased one of them. The numbers $2$, $3$, $4$, $-5$ remained, in some order. Recover the erased number and prove that it was exactly this number that was written.

For given values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ it turned out that the graphs of the functions $y=2a+\frac{1}{x-b}$ and $y=2c+\frac{1}{x-d}$ have exactly one common point. Prove that the graphs of the functions $y=2b+\frac{1}{x-a}$ and $y=2d+\frac{1}{x-c}$ also have exactly one common point.

In a triangle $ABC$ the altitudes or their extensions meet at the point $H$, and $R$ is the radius of its circumscribed circle. Prove that if $\angle A\leqslant\angle B\leqslant\angle C$, then $AH+BH\geqslant 2R$.

$n$ people came to a meeting ($n>1$). It turned out that any two of them have among those present exactly two other common acquaintances.

a) Prove that each of them is acquainted with the same number of people at this meeting.

b) Show that $n$ can be greater than $4$.

For $n=1, 2, 3$ we call a number of the $n$-th type any number that either is equal to $0$, or belongs to the infinite geometric progression $1, (n+2), (n+2)^2, \ldots$, or is the sum of several distinct terms of it. Prove that every natural number can be represented as the sum of a number of the first type, a number of the second type and a number of the third type.

About an infinite set of rectangles it is known that for every number $S$ it contains rectangles of total area greater than $S$.

a) Is it necessarily possible to cover the whole plane with this set, if overlaps are allowed?

b) The same question, if it is additionally known that all the rectangles in the set are squares.

Two digits were appended on the right to each term of some finite sequence of consecutive natural numbers, and a sequence of squares of consecutive natural numbers was obtained. What is the largest number of terms this sequence could have?

On a flat horizontal platform stand $5$ searchlights, each of which emits a laser beam at one of two acute angles $\alpha$ or $\beta$ to the platform and can rotate only about the vertical axis passing through the vertex of the beam. It is known that any $4$ of these searchlights can be turned so that all $4$ beams they emit meet at one point. Is it necessarily possible to turn all $5$ searchlights so that all $5$ beams meet at one point?

A teacher wrote on the board, in alphabetical order, all possible $2^n$ words consisting of $n$ letters A or B. Then he replaced each word by a product of $n$ factors, changing each letter A into $x$ and each letter B into $(1-x)$, and added together several of the first of these polynomials in $x$. Prove that the resulting polynomial is either a constant or an increasing function of $x$ on the segment $[0;1]$.

After dinner, dark stains of total area $S$ remained on a transparent square tablecloth. It turned out that if the tablecloth is folded in half along either of the two lines joining the midpoints of its opposite sides, or along one of its two diagonals, then the total visible area of the stains is $S_1$. But if the tablecloth is folded in half along its other diagonal, the total visible area of the stains remains equal to $S$. What is the smallest value the quantity $S_1:S$ can take?

Denote by $S(n,k)$ the number of coefficients of the expansion of the polynomial $(x+1)^n$ in powers of $x$ that are not divisible by $k$.

a) Find $S(2012,3)$.

b) Prove that $S(2012^{2011},2011)$ is divisible by $2012$.

Two monic quadratic trinomials have a common root, and the discriminant of their sum is equal to the sum of their discriminants. Prove that then the discriminant of at least one of these two trinomials is equal to zero.
Find all pairs of primes $p$ and $q$ with the following property: $7p+1$ is divisible by $q$, and $7q+1$ is divisible by $p$.

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given such that $AB=BC$ and $AD=DC$. The points $K$, $L$ and $M$ are the midpoints of the segments $AB$, $CD$ and $AC$ respectively. The perpendicular drawn from the point $A$ to the line $BC$ meets the perpendicular drawn from the point $C$ to the line $AD$ at the point $H$. Prove that the lines $KL$ and $HM$ are perpendicular.

Is it possible to colour all the cells of an infinite squared plane white and black so that every vertical line and every horizontal line meets finitely many white cells, and every inclined line meets finitely many black cells?

Three athletes started simultaneously from a point $A$ and ran along a straight line to a point $B$, each with his own constant speed. Having reached the point $B$, each of them instantly turned back and ran with another constant speed to the finish at the point $A$. Their coach ran alongside and was all the time at the point the sum of whose distances to the participants of the race was the smallest. It is known that the distance from $A$ to $B$ is $60$ m and that all the athletes finished simultaneously. Could the coach have run less than $100$ m?

Two teams of chess players with equal numbers of players played a match: each played one game with each member of the other team. In each game $1$ point was given for a win, $\frac{1}{2}$ for a draw and $0$ for a loss. In the end the teams scored equal numbers of points. Prove that some two participants of the match also scored equal numbers of points, if both teams had: a) $5$ players each; b) an arbitrary equal number of players.

Two pirates were dividing loot consisting of five gold ingots, one of which has mass $1$ kg and another $2$ kg. What mass could the other three ingots have had, if it is known that whichever two ingots the first pirate chooses for himself, the second pirate can divide the remaining ingots so that each of them gets the same amount of gold?
Find a value $a>1$ for which the equation $a^x=\log_a x$ has a unique solution.

Compare the numbers
$$\left(1+\frac{2}{3^3}\right)\left(1+\frac{2}{5^3}\right)\ldots\left(1+\frac{2}{2013^3}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}.$$

It is known that every triangular pyramid whose opposite edges are pairwise equal can be cut along three of its edges and unfolded so that its development is a triangle without interior cuts (see the figure). Is there any other convex polyhedron that can be cut along several of its edges and unfolded so that its development is a triangle without interior cuts?

The quadratic trinomial $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ takes values of different signs at the points $c$ and $\frac{1}{a}$. Prove that the roots of the trinomial $f(x)$ have different signs.

Find all values of $a$ for which there exist $x$, $y$ and $z$ such that the numbers $\cos x$, $\cos y$ and $\cos z$ are pairwise distinct and form, in the indicated order, an arithmetic progression, while the numbers $\cos(x+a)$, $\cos(y+a)$ and $\cos(z+a)$ also form, in the indicated order, an arithmetic progression.

On the sides $AD$ and $CD$ of a parallelogram $ABCD$ with centre $O$ the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively are marked such that $\angle AOP=\angle COQ=\angle ABC$.

a) Prove that $\angle ABP=\angle CBQ$.

b) Prove that the lines $AQ$ and $CP$ meet on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.

Sasha discovered that exactly $n$ working digit keys remained on his calculator. It turned out that every natural number from $1$ to $99\,999\,999$ can either be typed using only the working digits, or be obtained as the sum of two natural numbers each of which can be typed using only the working digits. What is the smallest $n$ for which this is possible?

A polynomial $P(x)$ has the following properties: $P(0)=1$ and $(P(x))^2=1+x+x^{100}Q(x)$ for all real $x$, where $Q(x)$ is some polynomial. Prove that the coefficient of $x^{99}$ in the polynomial $(P(x)+1)^{100}$ is equal to zero.

In a kingdom some pairs of cities are connected by a railway. The king has a complete list in which all such pairs are listed by name (each city has its own name). It turned out that for any ordered pair of cities the prince can rename all the cities so that the first city gets the name of the second city, and the king would not notice any changes. Is it true that for any pair of cities the prince can rename all the cities so that the first city gets the name of the second city, the second city gets the name of the first city, and the king would not notice any changes?

Is there a quadratic trinomial $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$ with integer coefficients and $a$ not divisible by $2014$ such that all the numbers $f(1), f(2), \ldots, f(2014)$ have different remainders upon division by $2014$? Justify your answer.
Find all $a$ and $b$ such that $|a|+|b|\geqslant 2/\sqrt{3}$ and the inequality $|a\sin x+b\sin(2x)|\leqslant 1$ holds for all $x$.
Prove that for every natural $n$ there is a natural number the decimal representation of whose square begins with $n$ ones and ends with some combination of $n$ ones and twos.

A chef has ten kitchen boys under him, some of whom are friends with each other. Every working day the chef assigns one or several kitchen boys to duty, and each of the boys on duty carries away from work one cake for each of his friends who is not on duty. At the end of the day the chef learns the number of missing cakes. Can he find out in $45$ working days which of the kitchen boys are friends with each other and which are not?

The surface of a convex polyhedron $A_1B_1C_1A_2B_2C_2$ consists of eight triangular faces $A_iB_jC_k$, where $i$, $j$, $k$ range from $1$ to $2$. A sphere with centre at the point $O$ touches all these faces. Prove that the point $O$ and the midpoints of the three segments $A_1A_2$, $B_1B_2$ and $C_1C_2$ lie in one plane.
A sequence $(a_n)$ is such that $a_n=n^2$ for $1\leqslant n\leqslant 5$ and for all natural $n$ the equality $a_{n+5}+a_{n+1}=a_{n+4}+a_n$ holds. Find $a_{2015}$.

Last year Misha bought a smartphone that cost a whole four-digit number of roubles. Going into the shop this year, he noticed that the price of the smartphone had increased by $20\%$ and consists of the same digits, but in reverse order. How much did Misha spend on the smartphone?

On the base $AC$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ an arbitrary point $X$ was taken, and on the lateral sides the points $P$ and $Q$ such that $XPBQ$ is a parallelogram. Prove that the point $Y$ symmetric to the point $X$ with respect to $PQ$ lies on the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.
A unit square is cut into $n$ triangles. Prove that one of the triangles can cover a square with side $1/n$.

Prove that it is impossible to place the natural numbers from $1$ to $64$ (each exactly once) in an $8\times 8$ table so that for every $2\times 2$ square of the form $\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline a&b\\ \hline c&d\\ \hline\end{array}$ the equality $|ad-bc|=1$ holds.

All faces of a hexahedron are quadrilaterals, and three edges meet at each of its vertices. Is it true that if it has an inscribed sphere and a circumscribed sphere whose centres coincide, then this hexahedron is a cube?

The sum of several not necessarily distinct positive numbers did not exceed $100$. Each of them was replaced by a new one as follows: first its logarithm to base $10$ was taken, then it was rounded in the standard way to the nearest integer, and finally $10$ was raised to the integer power found. Could the sum of the new numbers exceed $300$?

What is the largest number of factors of the form $\sin\frac{n\pi}{x}$ that can be crossed out on the left-hand side of the equation
$$\sin\frac{\pi}{x}\sin\frac{2\pi}{x}\sin\frac{3\pi}{x}\ldots\sin\frac{2015\pi}{x}=0$$
so that the number of its natural roots does not change?

Ivan Tsarevich has two vessels of capacity $1$ litre each; one of them is completely filled with ordinary water, and the other contains $a$ litres of living water, $0<a<1$. He can pour from vessel to vessel any volume of liquid up to any level without overflowing, and he wants, in a finite number of such pourings, to obtain a $40$-percent solution of living water in one of the vessels. For what values of $a$ can Ivan Tsarevich do this? Assume that the level of liquid in each of the vessels can be measured exactly at any moment.

A day in Anchuria can be either clear, when the sun shines all day, or rainy, when it rains all day. If today is not like yesterday, the Anchurians say that the weather has changed. Once Anchurian scientists established that January 1 is always clear, and each following day in January will be clear only if exactly one year earlier the weather changed on that day. In 2015 January in Anchuria was very varied: now sun, now rain. In which year will the weather in January for the first time change in exactly the same way as in January 2015?

On the surface of a spherical planet there are four continents separated from one another by ocean. Call a point of the ocean special if it has at least three nearest points of land (at equal distances from it), all on different continents. What is the largest number of special points that can be on this planet?

In a chess tournament for $12$ participants each played exactly one game with each of the others. A win gave $1$ point, a draw $\frac{1}{2}$, a loss $0$. Vasya lost only one game but took last place, scoring fewer points than everybody else. Petya took first place, scoring more points than everybody else. By how many points did Vasya trail Petya?
Is there a value of $x$ for which the equality $\arcsin^2x+\arccos^2x=1$ holds?

Inside a trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AD$ and $BC$ the points $M$ and $N$ are marked such that $AM=CN$ and $BM=DN$, and the quadrilaterals $AMND$ and $BMNC$ are cyclic. Prove that the line $MN$ is parallel to the bases of the trapezoid.

In an English club $n$ of its members ($n\geqslant 3$) gathered one evening. By the traditions of the club, each brought with him juice of the kind he prefers, in the amount he plans to drink during the evening. According to the rules of the club, at any moment any three of its members may sit down at a table and drink juice (each his own) in any amount, but necessarily all three equally. Prove that in order for all the members to be able to drink up completely the juice they brought during the evening, it is necessary and sufficient that the share of juice brought by any member of the club does not exceed one third of the total amount.

Can a cube with edge $1$ be cut by four planes into parts so that for each of the parts the distance between any two of its points is: a) less than $4/5$; b) less than $4/7$? It is assumed that all the planes are drawn simultaneously and that the cube and its parts do not move.

$N$ natives crossed from the left bank of a river to the right one using a single boat, each time sailing to the right in pairs and back alone. Initially each knew one joke, each his own. On the banks they told no jokes, but in the boat each told his fellow passenger all the jokes known to him at that moment. For each natural $k$ find the smallest possible value of $N$ for which it could happen that in the end each native knew, besides his own, at least $k$ jokes.
Find the smallest natural number the decimal representation of whose square ends in $2016$.

There is a balance with two pans, which is in equilibrium if the difference of the masses on its pans does not exceed $1$ g, and also weights of masses $\ln 3, \ln 4, \ldots, \ln 79$ g. Is it possible to place all these weights on the pans of the balance so that the balance is in equilibrium?
Is it possible to mark $k$ vertices of a regular $14$-gon so that every quadrilateral with vertices at the marked points having two parallel sides is a rectangle, if: a) $k=6$; b) $k\geqslant 7$?

In some time a boy rode a bicycle a whole number of times around the perimeter of a square school in one direction with speed of constant magnitude $10$ km/h. In the same time his father walked around the perimeter of the school with speed $5$ km/h, and he could change the direction of motion. The father saw the boy at those and only those moments when they were on the same side of the school. Could the father see the boy for more than half of the indicated time?

About the monic polynomial
$$P(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\ldots+a_1x+a_0$$
with real coefficients it is known that for some natural $m\geqslant 2$ the polynomial
$$\underbrace{P(P(\ldots P}_{m\text{ times}}(x)\ldots))$$
has real roots, and only positive ones. Must the polynomial $P(x)$ itself have real roots, and only positive ones?
Find the smallest natural number divisible by $80$ in which one can interchange two of its distinct digits so that the resulting number is also divisible by $80$.

On the incircle of a triangle $ABC$, which touches the side $AC$ at the point $S$, there is a point $Q$ such that the midpoints of the segments $AQ$ and $QC$ also lie on the incircle. Prove that $QS$ is the bisector of the angle $AQC$.

Let $x_0$ be the positive root of the equation $x^{2017}-x-1=0$, and $y_0$ the positive root of the equation $y^{4034}-y=3x_0$.

a) Compare $x_0$ and $y_0$.

b) Find the tenth digit after the decimal point of the number $|x_0-y_0|$.

Three cyclists ride in the same direction along a circular track of length $300$ metres. Each of them moves with his own constant speed, all the speeds being different. A photographer can take a successful picture of the cyclists if they all find themselves on some section of the track of length $d$ metres. For what smallest $d$ will the photographer be sure to be able, sooner or later, to take a successful picture?
On the faces of a unit cube $8$ points are marked that are the vertices of a smaller cube. Find all values that the edge length of this cube can take.

In Chicago $36$ criminal gangs operate, some of which are at enmity with each other. Each gangster belongs to several gangs, and any two gangsters belong to different sets of gangs. It is known that no gangster belongs to two gangs that are at enmity with each other. Moreover, it turned out that each gang to which some gangster does not belong is at enmity with some gang to which this gangster belongs. What is the largest number of gangsters there can be in Chicago?

Two non-constant progressions $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ are given, one of which is arithmetic and the other geometric. It is known that $a_1=b_1$, $a_2:b_2=2$ and $a_4:b_4=8$. What can the ratio $a_3:b_3$ be equal to?

Dunno is acquainted only with decimal logarithms and believes that the logarithm of the sum of two numbers is equal to the product of their logarithms, and the logarithm of the difference of two numbers is equal to the quotient of their logarithms. Can Dunno find at least one pair of numbers for which both of these equalities are indeed true simultaneously?

Detective Nero Wolfe is investigating a crime. $80$ people are involved in the case, among whom one is the criminal and another one is a witness of the crime (but it is not known who they are). Every day the detective may invite one or several of these $80$ people, and if among those invited there is the witness but not the criminal, the witness will tell who the criminal is. Can the detective be sure to solve the case in $12$ days?

Inside a triangle $ABC$ a point $D$ is taken such that $BD=CD$ and $\angle BDC=120^\circ$. Outside the triangle $ABC$ a point $E$ is taken such that $AE=CE$, $\angle AEC=60^\circ$, and the points $B$ and $E$ lie in different half-planes with respect to $AC$. Prove that $\angle AFD=90^\circ$, where $F$ is the midpoint of the segment $BE$.

A $2017\times 2017$ table is filled with nonzero digits. Among the $4034$ numbers whose decimal representations coincide with the rows and columns of this table, read from left to right and from top to bottom respectively, all except one are divisible by a prime number $p$, and the remaining number is not divisible by $p$. Find all possible values of $p$.
The graphs of a quadratic trinomial and of its derivative divide the coordinate plane into four parts. How many roots does this quadratic trinomial have?

There are one triangular and one quadrilateral pyramid, all of whose edges are equal to $1$. Show how to cut them into several parts and glue a cube from these parts (without voids or gaps; all the parts must be used).

Do there exist a natural number $n$ and a polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $n$ having $n$ distinct real roots such that for all real $x$ the equality

a) $P(x)P(x+1)=P(x^2)$;

b) $P(x)P(x+1)=P(x^2+1)$

holds?
Can the number $11^{2018}$ be represented as the sum of the cubes of two natural numbers?

On the sides of a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ the equilateral triangles $ABC_1$, $BCD_1$, $CDE_1$, $DEF_1$, $EFA_1$ and $FAB_1$ are constructed outward. It turned out that the triangle $B_1D_1F_1$ is equilateral. Prove that the triangle $A_1C_1E_1$ is also equilateral.

In a house of $2^n$ rooms a renovation was done. The light switches turned out to be mixed up, so that when the switch in one room is turned on, the light comes on, generally speaking, in some other room. To find out which switch is connected to which room, the foreman sends several people into some rooms so that they, having simultaneously turned on the switches there, come back and report whether the light was on in their room or not.

a) Prove that the foreman can establish the correspondence between switches and rooms with $2n$ such dispatches.

b) Can he manage with $2n-1$ such dispatches?

Solve the equation
$$x^3+(\log_2 5+\log_3 2+\log_5 3)x=(\log_2 3+\log_3 5+\log_5 2)x^2+1.$$

Some dominoes, each covering exactly two cells, were placed without overlapping on a $2018\times 2018$ board. It turned out that no two dominoes have a common whole side, i.e. no two form either a $2\times 2$ square or a $4\times 1$ rectangle. Can more than $99\%$ of all the cells of the board be covered under these conditions?

Let $x$ and $y$ be five-digit numbers in whose decimal representations all ten digits are used exactly once each. Find the largest possible value of $x$ if $\operatorname{tg}x^\circ-\operatorname{tg}y^\circ=1+\operatorname{tg}x^\circ\operatorname{tg}y^\circ$ ($x^\circ$ denotes the angle of $x$ degrees).

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA_1$ and $CC_1$ are drawn. The circle circumscribed about the triangle $A_1BC_1$ passes through the point $M$ of intersection of the medians. Find all possible values of the angle $B$.

Zhenya painted a spherical egg successively in five paints, dipping it into a glass with the next paint so that exactly half of the surface area of the egg (a hemisphere) was painted. As a result the egg was painted completely. Prove that one of the paints was superfluous, i.e. if Zhenya had not used this paint and had dipped the egg into the other paints in the same way, it would still have been painted completely.

Let $f(x)=x^2+3x+2$. Compute
$$\left(1-\frac{2}{f(1)}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{f(2)}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{f(3)}\right)\ldots\left(1-\frac{2}{f(2019)}\right).$$

A natural number divisible by $7$ is printed on a computer screen, and the cursor is in the gap between some two neighbouring digits of it. Prove that there is a digit such that if it is typed into this gap any number of times, all the resulting numbers will also be divisible by $7$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA'$ and $BB'$ are drawn. The point $O$ is the centre of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the distance from the point $A'$ to the line $BO$ is equal to the distance from the point $B'$ to the line $AO$.
Prove that for any distinct natural numbers $m$ and $n$ the inequality $\left|\sqrt[n]{m}-\sqrt[m]{n}\right|>\frac{1}{mn}$ holds.

The orthogonal projection of a tetrahedron onto the plane of one of its faces is a trapezoid of area $1$. Can the orthogonal projection of this tetrahedron onto the plane of another of its faces be a square of area $1$?

Consider on the squared plane the broken lines starting at the point $(0,0)$ with vertices at points with integer coordinates such that each successive link goes along the sides of the cells either upwards or to the right. To each such broken line there corresponds a worm: the figure consisting of the cells of the plane that have at least one common point with this broken line. Prove that the number of worms that can be divided into two-cell dominoes in exactly $n>2$ different ways is equal to the number of natural numbers less than $n$ and coprime to $n$. (Worms are different if they consist of different sets of cells.)
Using the equality $\lg 11=1.0413\ldots$, find the smallest number $n>1$ for which among the $n$-digit numbers there is none equal to some natural power of the number $11$.
Is there a hyperbola given by an equation of the form $y=\frac{a}{x}$ under which, in the first coordinate quadrant ($x>0$, $y>0$), there lie exactly $82$ points with integer coordinates?

The faces of the polyhedron shown in the figure are four regular pentagons, four triangles and two squares. How many times is the side of the upper square larger than the side of the lower one?

Prove that for every natural number $n\geqslant 2$ and for any real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ satisfying the condition $a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n\ne 0$, the equation
$$a_1(x-a_2)(x-a_3)\ldots(x-a_n)+a_2(x-a_1)(x-a_3)\ldots(x-a_n)+\ldots+a_n(x-a_1)(x-a_2)\ldots(x-a_{n-1})=0$$
has at least one real root.

Several numbers are written on a board. It is allowed to erase any two numbers $a$ and $b$ and then write the number $\frac{a+b}{4}$ instead of one of them. What is the smallest number that can remain on the board after $2018$ such operations, if initially $2019$ ones are written on it?
Give an example of a number divisible by $2020$ in which each of the ten digits occurs the same number of times.
Is there a non-periodic function $f$ defined on the whole number line such that for every $x$ the equality $f(x+1)=f(x+1)f(x)+1$ holds?

In an acute triangle $ABC$ ($AB<BC$) the altitude $BH$ is drawn. The point $P$ is symmetric to the point $H$ with respect to the line joining the midpoints of the sides $AC$ and $BC$. Prove that the line $BP$ contains the centre of the circumscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$.

$10$ cells were cut out of an $8\times 8$ chessboard. It is known that among the cut-out cells there are both black and white ones. What is the largest number of two-cell rectangles that can then be guaranteed to be cut out of this board?
Is there a tetrahedron whose sections by two different planes are squares $1\times 1$ and $100\times 100$?

$2n$ consecutive integers are written on a board. In one move one may divide the written numbers into pairs in an arbitrary way and replace each pair of numbers by the sum and the difference of the numbers of this pair (it is not necessary to subtract the smaller number from the larger one; all the replacements occur simultaneously). Prove that $2n$ consecutive numbers will never again appear on the board.

A boy rides a scooter from one bus stop to another and looks in the mirror to see whether a bus has appeared behind him. As soon as the boy notices the bus, he can change the direction of motion. For what largest distance between the stops is the boy guaranteed not to miss the bus, if he knows that he rides with a speed three times smaller than the speed of the bus and is able to see the bus at a distance of at most $2$ km?

Solve the equation
$$\operatorname{tg}\pi x=\left[\lg\pi^x\right]-\left[\lg\left[\pi^x\right]\right],$$
where $[a]$ denotes the largest integer not exceeding $a$.

$15$ gnomes sit at a round rotating table on which there are $8$ white and $7$ black cups. They have put on $8$ white and $7$ black caps. Each gnome takes a cup whose colour coincides with the colour of his cap and puts it in front of himself, after which the table is rotated at random. What is the largest number of coincidences of the colours of cup and cap that can be guaranteed after the rotation of the table (the gnomes themselves choose how to sit, but do not know how the table will turn)?

On the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$ a point $D$ is taken such that the angle $BDC$ is equal to the angle $ABC$. What is the smallest possible distance between the centres of the circles circumscribed about the triangles $ABC$ and $ABD$, if $BC=1$?

A grasshopper jumps along the number line, on which the points $-a$ and $b$ are marked. It is known that $a$ and $b$ are positive numbers whose ratio is irrational. If the grasshopper is at a point that is closer to $-a$, it jumps to the right by a distance equal to $a$. If it is at the midpoint of the segment $[-a;b]$ or at a point closer to $b$, it jumps to the left by a distance equal to $b$. Prove that regardless of its initial position the grasshopper at some moment will be at a distance less than $10^{-6}$ from the point $0$.

A natural number is written on a board. If its last digit (in the units place) is erased, a nonzero number remains that is divisible by $20$, and if its first digit is erased, the remaining number is divisible by $21$. What is the smallest number that can be written on the board if its second digit is not equal to $0$?

Is there a function $f$ defined on the segment $[-1;1]$ that satisfies for all real $x$ the equality
$$2f(\cos x)=f(\sin x)+\sin x\,?$$

The point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. A circle $\omega$ passes through the point $A$, touches the line $BC$ at the point $M$ and meets the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $D$ and $E$ respectively. The points $X$ and $Y$ are the midpoints of the segments $BE$ and $CD$ respectively. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle $MXY$ touches the circle $\omega$.

A country has $100$ cities, connected by a network of roads such that from any city to any other one can travel in only one way without U-turns. The layout of the road network is known; forks and intersections of the network are not necessarily cities, and every dead-end branch of the network necessarily ends in a city. A navigator can measure the length of the path along this network between any two cities. Is it possible to determine with certainty the length of the whole road network with $100$ such measurements?

The polyhedron with vertices at the midpoints of the edges of a cube is called a cuboctahedron. A section of a cuboctahedron by a plane is a regular polygon. What is the largest number of sides it can have?

The upper integer part of a number $x$ is the smallest integer greater than or equal to $x$. Is there a number $A$ such that for every natural $n$ the distance from the upper integer part of $A^n$ to the nearest square of a natural number is always equal to $2$?
The polynomial $P(x)=x^3+ax^2+bx+c$ has three distinct real roots, the largest of which is equal to the sum of the other two. Prove that $c>ab$.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the point $O$ is the centre of the circumscribed circle. The point $B_1$ is symmetric to the point $B$ with respect to the side $AC$. The lines $AO$ and $B_1C$ meet at the point $K$. Prove that the ray $KA$ is the bisector of the angle $BKB_1$.
Find the smallest natural number $N>9$ that is not divisible by $7$, but such that if any of its digits is replaced by a seven, the resulting number is divisible by $7$.
Is there a convex quadrilateral whose side lengths and diagonal lengths, in some order, form a geometric progression?

In a laboratory, $120$ outwardly indistinguishable test tubes stand on a shelf; $118$ of them contain a neutral substance, one contains poison and one contains antidote. The test tubes got mixed up at random, and one needs to find the test tube with the poison and the test tube with the antidote. For this one can use the services of an outside testing laboratory, to which several mixtures of liquids from any number of test tubes (one drop from each tube) are sent simultaneously, and for each mixture the laboratory will report the result: $+1$ if the mixture contains poison and no antidote; $-1$ if the mixture contains antidote but no poison; $0$ in the remaining cases. Is it possible, having prepared $19$ such mixtures and sent them to the laboratory in a single parcel, to determine with certainty from the reported results which test tube contains the poison and which the antidote?

Alik's collection contains two types of items: badges and bracelets. There are more badges than bracelets. Alik noticed that if he increased the number of bracelets by some (not necessarily integer) factor, without changing the number of badges, his collection would contain $100$ items. And if, conversely, he increased the original number of badges by the same factor, leaving the number of bracelets unchanged, he would have $101$ items. How many badges and how many bracelets could there have been in Alik's collection?

In a Cartesian coordinate system (with the same scale on the $x$ and $y$ axes) the graph of the exponential function $y=3^x$ was drawn. Then the $y$-axis and all the marks on the $x$-axis were erased. Only the graph of the function and the $x$-axis without scale and without the mark $0$ remained. How can the $y$-axis be reconstructed with compass and ruler?

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the bisector $AL$ is drawn. On the extension of the segment $LA$ beyond the point $A$ a point $K$ is chosen such that $AK=AL$. The circumcircles of the triangles $BLK$ and $CLK$ meet the segments $AC$ and $AB$ at the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Prove that the lines $PQ$ and $BC$ are parallel.

A starship is in a half-space at distance $a$ from its boundary. The crew knows this but has no idea in which direction to move in order to reach the boundary plane. The starship can fly in space along any trajectory, measuring the length of the path travelled, and has a sensor that gives a signal when the boundary is reached. Can the starship be guaranteed to reach the boundary, covering a path of length at most $14a$?
A polynomial of degree $2022$ with integer coefficients and leading coefficient $1$ is given. What is the largest number of roots it can have in the interval $(0;1)$?

A sultan gathered $300$ court sages and proposed a test to them. There are caps of $25$ different colours, known to the sages in advance. The sultan announced that each of the sages would be given one of these caps, and that if for each colour the number of caps put on is written down, all these numbers will be distinct. Each sage will see the caps of the other sages but not his own. Then all the sages will simultaneously announce the supposed colour of their own cap. Can the sages agree in advance to act so that it is guaranteed that at least $150$ of them name the colour correctly?
Some non-negative numbers $a, b, c$ satisfy the equality $a+b+c=2\sqrt{abc}$. Prove that $bc\geqslant b+c$.

A volleyball championship with $16$ teams was held as a single round robin (each team played each other team exactly once; there are no draws in volleyball). It turned out that some two teams won the same number of games. Prove that there are three teams that beat one another cyclically (that is, $A$ beat $B$, $B$ beat $C$, and $C$ beat $A$).

In a convex $12$-gon all the angles are equal. It is known that the lengths of some ten of its sides are equal to $1$, and the length of one more is equal to $2$. What can the area of this $12$-gon be?

In an isosceles trapezoid a diagonal is drawn. Along the contour of each of the two resulting triangles crawls its own beetle. The speeds of the beetles are constant and equal. The beetles do not change the direction in which they go around their contours, and along the diagonal of the trapezoid they crawl in different directions. Prove that for any initial positions of the beetles they will meet at some time.

Tanya successively wrote out the numbers of the form $n^7-1$ for natural numbers $n=2, 3, \ldots$ and noticed that for $n=8$ the resulting number is divisible by $337$. For what smallest $n>1$ will she obtain a number divisible by $2022$?

Tangents to the graphs of the functions $y=\cos x$ and $y=a\operatorname{tg}x$ were drawn at some point of their intersection. Prove that these tangents are perpendicular to each other for every $a\ne 0$.

Let $ABCD$ be a parallelogram different from a rectangle, and let a point $P$ be chosen inside it such that the circumcircles of the triangles $PAB$ and $PCD$ have a common chord perpendicular to $AD$. Prove that the radii of these circles are equal.
A polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $n>5$ with integer coefficients having $n$ distinct integer roots is given. Prove that the polynomial $P(x)+3$ has $n$ distinct real roots.

More than $4$ players took part in a tennis tournament (in which there are no draws). On each playing day each tennis player took part in exactly one game. By the end of the tournament each had played each other exactly once. Call a player persistent if he won at least one match and after his first win never lost. Call the remaining players non-persistent. Is it true that the playing days on which there was a game between non-persistent players are more than half of all the days?
The midpoints of all the altitudes of some tetrahedron lie on its inscribed sphere. Is it true that the tetrahedron is regular?

Call a triple of numbers a triplet if one of them is equal to the arithmetic mean of the other two. The sequence $(a_n)$ is constructed as follows: $a_1=a_2=1$, and for $n>2$ the number $a_n$ is the smallest natural number such that among the numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ there are no three forming a triplet. Prove that $a_n\leqslant\frac{n^2+7}{8}$ for every $n$.

A strictly increasing function $f\colon\mathbb{N}_0\to\mathbb{N}_0$ is given (where $\mathbb{N}_0$ is the set of non-negative integers) that satisfies the relation $f(n+f(m))=f(n)+m+1$ for all $m, n\in\mathbb{N}_0$. Find all the values that $f(2023)$ can take.
What is the smallest number of distinct integers that must be taken so that among them one can choose both a geometric and an arithmetic progression of length $5$?

In a triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $BE$ and $CF$ meet at the point $H$, the point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $BC$, and $X$ is the point of intersection of the internal common tangents to the circles inscribed in the triangles $BMF$ and $CME$. Prove that the points $X$, $M$ and $H$ lie on one line.

There is an absolutely precise two-pan balance and a set of $50$ weights whose weights are $\operatorname{arctg}1$, $\operatorname{arctg}\frac{1}{2}$, $\operatorname{arctg}\frac{1}{3}$, $\ldots$, $\operatorname{arctg}\frac{1}{50}$. Prove that one can choose $10$ of them and place $5$ weights on each of the pans so that the balance is in equilibrium.

For a convex polyhedron denote by $V$, $E$ and $T$ respectively the number of vertices, the number of edges and the largest number of triangular faces having a common vertex. Prove that $V\sqrt{E+T}\geqslant 2E$.

For example, for a tetrahedron ($V=4$, $E=6$, $T=3$) equality holds, while for a triangular prism ($V=6$, $E=9$, $T=1$) or a cube ($V=8$, $E=12$, $T=0$) the strict inequality holds.

A mathematician has $19$ distinct weights whose masses in kilograms are $\ln 2, \ln 3, \ln 4, \ldots, \ln 20$, and an absolutely precise two-pan balance. He placed several weights on the balance so that it was in equilibrium. What is the largest number of weights that could be on the balance?

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitude $AH$ is drawn. The points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of the segments $BH$ and $CH$. Prove that the point of intersection of the perpendiculars dropped from the points $M$ and $N$ to the lines $AB$ and $AC$ respectively is equidistant from the points $B$ and $C$.

There is a heap of $100$ stones. Two players play the following game. The first player takes $1$ stone, then the second may take $1$ or $2$ stones, then the first may take $1$, $2$ or $3$ stones, then the second $1$, $2$, $3$ or $4$ stones, and so on. The player who takes the last stone wins. Who can win regardless of how the opponent plays?

A polynomial of degree $n\geqslant 1$ with nonzero integer coefficients is given, each of which is a root of it. Prove that the absolute values of all the coefficients of this polynomial do not exceed $2$.

In a tetrahedron $ABCD$ opposite edges are pairwise equal. Through the midpoint of the segment $AH_A$, where $H_A$ is the point of intersection of the altitudes of the face $BCD$, the line $h_A$ is drawn perpendicular to the plane $BCD$. In the same way the points $H_B$, $H_C$, $H_D$ were defined and the lines $h_B$, $h_C$, $h_D$ were constructed for the three other faces of the tetrahedron respectively. Prove that the lines $h_A$, $h_B$, $h_C$, $h_D$ meet at one point.

Koschei devised a test for Ivan the Fool. He gave Ivan a magic pipe on which only two notes can be played, C and B. To pass the test Ivan must play some melody of $300$ notes of his choice. But before he begins to play, Koschei chooses and declares forbidden one melody of five notes, one of six notes, $\ldots$, one of $30$ notes. If at some moment the last notes played form one of the forbidden melodies, the pipe stops sounding. Can Ivan pass the test, whatever melodies Koschei declares forbidden?
Is there a point of the coordinate plane with respect to which the graph of the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{2^x+1}$ is symmetric?

A football championship was held in two rounds. In each round every team played every other team one match (three points are given for a win, one for a draw, zero for a loss). It turned out that all the teams together scored in the first round $60\%$ of the total sum of all the points for the two rounds. It is also known that the winner of the championship scored in the second round $30$ times fewer points than all the teams together in the first round. How many teams took part in the tournament?
Prove that if for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ the number $2+2\sqrt{12n^2+1}$ is an integer, then it is a perfect square.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AH_A$, $BH_B$ and $CH_C$ meet at the point $H$. Through the points at which the circle of radius $HH_A$ with centre $H$ meets the segments $BH$ and $CH$ the line $\ell_A$ is drawn. The lines $\ell_B$ and $\ell_C$ are drawn similarly. Prove that the orthocentre of the triangle formed by the lines $\ell_A$, $\ell_B$, $\ell_C$ coincides with the centre of the circle inscribed in the triangle $ABC$.

Petya and Vasya, independently of each other, divide a white $100\times 100$ squared board into arbitrary groups of cells, each consisting of an even (but not necessarily the same for all) number of cells, each into his own set of groups. Is it true that after this one can always paint half of the cells of each group of Petya's partition black so that each group of Vasya's partition contains equally many black and white cells?

$100$ participants gathered at a joint symposium of liars (who always lie) and truth-lovers (who always tell the truth); not all of them are liars and not all are truth-lovers. Every two participants are either acquainted or not acquainted with each other. Each answered "yes" or "no" to the question "Are you acquainted?" about each of the others. What is the smallest number of "yes" answers that could have been received?
A sequence $a_n=n!(n^2-2025n+1)$ is given for all natural $n$. Find the sum of the first $2025$ terms of this sequence.

Two triangular pyramids with a common base $ABC$ are given. Their apexes $S$ and $R$ lie on different sides of the plane $ABC$. All the lateral edges of one pyramid are parallel to the corresponding lateral faces of the other. Prove that the volume of one pyramid is twice the volume of the other.

Do there exist natural numbers $m$ and $n$ and a polynomial $f(x)$ with integer coefficients such that $f(m)$ is not divisible by $n$, but $f(p^k)$ is divisible by $n$ for every prime $p$ and every natural $k$?

The altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ of an acute triangle $ABC$ meet at the point $H$. The bisector of the angle $CBH$ meets the segment $CH$ at the point $X$, and the bisector of the angle $BCH$ meets the segment $BH$ at the point $Y$. Denote the angle $XA_1Y$ by $\alpha$. Define $\beta$ and $\gamma$ similarly. Find the value of the sum $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$.
